item.title: Restaurant Theft Adds to Rising Dining Costs
item.content:encoded: Bloomberg Pursuits Food Editor Kate Krader tells Bloomberg This Weekend that diners are taking everything from silverware and glassware to artwork and bathroom fixtures, adding replacement costs for restaurants already struggling with tight profit margins. Speaking with hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini, Krader also discusses the return of late night dining in cities including New York and London as restaurants extend their hours and customers embrace later reservations. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Stewards rule Piastri shares blame for Norris clash
item.author: Josh Suttill
item.content:encoded: Formula 1’s Singapore Grand Prix stewards determined that both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri contributed to their last-lap sprint race collision, so ruled that no further action was necessary. The stewards said Piastri hadn’t expected Norris to overtake him, but he "noticed [Norris] on the inside and attempted to leave space". "[Norris] said that he saw an opportunity to overtake and said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of [Piastri] prior to the apex, and therefore expected to be left space. "As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated, so he had to use the inside kerb and braked, and a collision occurred. "The stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision. "Therefore, the stewards determined to take no further action." Norris is right that he had his front axle ahead of the mirror of Piastri’s sister car at the apex of Turn 5, so he satisfies that aspect of F1’s racing rules.But it does not appear Piastri - who was caught unawares by the divebomb - had means of leaving more space at that corner; so once he turned in, a collision became inevitable.Given the stewards stated "both drivers had contributed to the incident", we can infer that Piastri’s not anticipating the overtake and leaving enough space is what he did wrong - whereas Norris was ambitious with his move and had to climb onto the inside kerb to try to complete it. The start of Norris’s interview with F1 broadcaster Viaplay after the sprint race made his feelings clear.Norris was asked: "You'll surely always want to finish as high as possible, but it’s also a sprint, P4 and P5 and it was your team-mate in front of you... Wasn’t it too unnecessary, that move?"He replied: "What, to go for a big gap? To overtake?". He followed up: "What's the title name of the race?"The interviewer replied, "sprint", to which Norris said: "Sprint. What’s [the word] after sprint?" - "race" came the reply.Norris smiled: "Wow! Good job. It’s a race". "We were just stuck the whole race and the last lap there was a big opportunity into [Turn] 5 so I went for it," Norris said in the media pen. "The gap closed a bit more than I would have liked and obviously I've had to back out of it because the gap was closing - so I've had to try and avoid the incident and obviously there still was one. But it was a big gap so I went for it, I have the right to do that. The rest we go review as a team." Piastri said "it’s for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, not that bothered either way, just a lot of work for the team to get both cars fixed, just a shame for the team". Meanwhile, Liam Lawson, having been shown a replay of the incident by Sky Sports F1’s Karun Chandhok, mused: "On the last lap, it’s not for many points; I don't think it's worth it". Perez dodges serving penalty for Stroll clashThere was a slightly unusual decision made in the assessment of another of the sprint’s incidents.Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll collided on the opening lap of the race when Perez tried to pass on the inside of the Turn 16 right-hander.The stewards felt Stroll had turned in reasonably for the corner and Perez was predominantly to blame after having a lock-up.They considered the tricky conditions reasonable mitigation and wanted to issue Perez with a five-second penalty instead of the usual 10.But Perez retired from the race - and according to the stewards a five-second penalty does not typically convert to a grid drop.Had it been a 10-second penalty, this would be different. So Perez escapes sanction for the clash.

item.title: Will Warner Bros. kill Skydance — or will David Ellison kill Warner Bros?
item.author: Nilay Patel
item.content:encoded: Today, I’m talking with Peter Kafka, chief correspondent at and host of the podcast, about the gigantic Warner Bros.-Paramount merger and the future of the company now simply called Skydance.Skydance is owned by David Ellison, son of Oracle CEO Larry Ellison, and its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery officially closed the day Peter and I spoke.There are some grand ambitions here, but the reality is that acquiring Warner never goes well for anyone. AOL failed, AT&T failed, and Discovery failed — although it did succeed in flipping these assets to Skydance. So I wanted to ask Peter if he thinks the Ellisons and Skydance have a real shot at succeeding where so many companies before them have hit the rocks. Okay: Peter Kafka on Warner Bros. and Skydance. Here we go.This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.Peter Kafka, you’re the chief correspondent at Business Insider, and you’re the host of thepodcast, our sister podcast here on the Vox Media Podcast Network. Welcome back toThanks for having me. It’s big media day again!A big media day. It’s an auspicious day, as my parents would say. It is the day that the Warner-Paramount merger closes. We’ve all been calling it Warner Mount, but I’m told this company will insteadEvery time I see the word Skydance, I assume it is foreign-owned, which is maybe true in some way.Another way to think of it is that there are iconic names in Hollywood. Paramount is such an iconic name that Viacom turned itself into Paramount years ago. Warner Bros. is a legendary studio. Let’s get rid of those names. Let’s add Skydance, which no one’s ever heard of.Let’s just start at the start. There was Paramount. There’s Warner Bros. The deal closes today. That is all going to be a new company called Skydance. Is Skydance just a holding company? Are we as consumers meant to know that this thing exists?I think for the near term, you’re still gonna think of companies like Paramount, Warner Bros., and HBO as brands you know, but this is going to be one company. They’re going to merge everything. They’re likely going to merge the streaming services, Paramount and HBO, into a thing, not right away, but eventually. So I do think Skydance will be a name that consumers will probably know at some point.I just have to ask, what are the chances that HBO Max will be rebranded yet again into Skydance?There’s probably gonna be some branding stuff. Not again. In the near term, because this is still a cable TV company, there are actually some limits on what these guys can do with their brands and their services. And they won’t come out and say, “We’re gonna mush this stuff together.”But there’s likely to be one mega streaming service, and maybe you can get HBO separately, or maybe you can only get HBO or only Paramount. Still, it’s gonna be one thing, and one movie studio. It’s all gonna get mushed together, and it’s all gonna be run by David Ellison.David Ellison is just the latest to believe that he can buy Warner Bros. and make something good happen. I have joked many times on this show that maybe the only antitrust policy this country needs is to make it illegal to buy Warner Bros., and that would just solve a lot of problems. Why does he think he will be successful?Well, his dad’s the eighth richest man in the world, so that’s not nothing.That Oracle stock is tied up in a bunch of AI stuff. It’s moving up and down.We can talk about that. But one, that means that he literally has the money to buy this, and two, that this is a public company kind of in name only. David Ellison and Larry Ellison, his father, control this company effectively. They don’t really need to worry that much about equity shareholders. Debt’s a different issue. And he’s 43. He’s got a long run backed by tens of billions of dollars of his father’s money to take a stab at this. And as you said, he will not be the first person to do this. There’s a long list of failures. I think maybe that’s appealing to guys like him. It’s like, “Everyone else is dumb. I’m the smart guy who’s gonna figure it out.”“Everyone else is dumb, and I’m smarter than everyone else is,” is very appealing. But that long list of failures, if you just look at it — they’re all shaped like this idea. We’re gonna take iconic Warner Bros. content, we’re gonna marry it to new distribution, we’re gonna reduce the overhead and costs and decadence of Hollywood. Where does new revenue come from?There’s no plan for new revenue. There’s no plan for new revenue. Right now it’s shrinking; it’s cutting costs. It’s when we merge these two companies together, we’re gonna save $6 billion over the next three years. We promise that most of that’s not gonna come from layoffs, but a lot of it’s gonna come from layoffs.These are companies that have had many, many rounds of layoffs prior to this. And you could argue, well, there’s probably not that much more to cut. I think reasonably you could say, look, if you combine two big streaming operations, two big studio operations, there probably is stuff [to cut]. You can probably sell off some real estate. You probably don’t need all the executives you currently have. There’s some savings there. But how do you grow? No idea. And no one’s really articulated that.Growth is required for a couple of reasons here. One, yes, there are going to be shareholders; people will be looking at it. There’s David Ellison’s ego. Then there’s debt. This deal is levered to the max, right?Eighty billion dollars [in debt]. Eight zero. More important than the number is the reason that David Ellison was able to buy Warner Bros. was that the last owner couldn’t deal with the debt that he took on to buy the company. And that was a mere $43 or $50 billion, depending on who was counting. This is David Zaslav, the former CEO of Warner Bros. Discovery, who spent his entire tenure running that company telling Wall Street that, yes, he was gonna get the debt down, and that was his main focus, and debt, debt, debt, reduce, reduce, reduce.I mean, he did reduce some debt, but he never convinced Wall Street that he had a plan to grow. Wall Street gave up on this company years ago, which is why when David Ellison decided he wanted to buy it, the stock was, like, seven bucks or something like that. Eventually bought it for, you know, many, many times that. And now David Zaslav is considered — or he considers himself — a genius for selling the company at such a high price. You could also argue, as someone told me yesterday, that a unicorn sort of manifested itself and allowed David Zaslav to exit the situation he had put himself into.I don’t know who the next unicorn will be for this company if David Ellison at some point decides, “Ugh, actually this is a lot of debt and a lot of pain. I don’t wanna do this anymore.”I want to come back to that because I have a little bit of a conspiracy theory. It’s a little bit supported by the attitudes of some of the players here, but we’ll come back around. Even the previous owner, AT&T, which is remarkable that AT&T was the… Somewhere in this chain of ownership, AT&T owned Warner.They could not deal with these assets. Their plan was to distribute Warner content on AT&T phones, which never made any sense. But they were a more aggressive owner.It also wasn’t really their plan. Their plan was, “Hey, Netflix is a really valuable company. The stock is very high. We’re this boring telecoms company. Our stock is not moving. What if we owned a [version of] Netflix? I bet Wall Street would reward us as a high-flying tech company all of a sudden.” And Wall Street didn’t. Within a couple of years, AT&T said, “Uh, oh yeah, no, we’re out of this.” And yes, they had said a bunch of stuff about mobile, connectivity, ads, and targeting, and none of that ever went anywhereI will never forget covering their antitrust case when they had to get approval for that deal. And oh, by the way, if the last guy’s project turns out to be successful, we’ll take credit for that. But we’re gonna bring in new stuff.” I don’t think Ted Sarandos was playing 3D/4D chess here. I think they thought this was a good idea. But I think the much more obvious answer is Wall Street hated the idea. Wall Street kept telling Netflix, “We hate this. We hate this. Please don’t spend $80 billion on this. And also, by the way, you’re gonna have a tough time getting this through regulation.” And I think Ted Sarandos eventually said, “Okay, you’re right.” I’ve seen him speak publicly about this and in other venues. He seems quite upset about the fact that he didn’t get this deal. I think there are also feelings involved here. But I don’t think this was all a master plan on their part. I think they went for it. They didn’t get it. They’re bummed out. They’re gonna move on.I think an angry, aggressive Netflix might actually be the best thing that could happen to Hollywood right now, because they were headed towards their own vertical video slop fest, and maybe now they’re not going to do that.I think that’s the question for — I mean, it’s a question for everybody. But for Netflix, it’s: you guys have been super successful for a couple of decades by doing one thing. Well, initially you were doing DVD by mail, then you went to streaming, and that’s all you did. And you didn’t ever sell movies. You didn’t do a la carte stuff. You didn’t do advertising. You didn’t do sports. Now you do advertising. Now you do sports. Now you’re doing games. Now you’re doing podcasts. Maybe you’re gonna integrate with other kinds of TV stuff. And so this laser focus that Netflix had, which proved very successful, they are moving away from. They may have to move away from it. They may have sort of reached the limit of that growth. But it gets trickier and trickier the more things you add to that stack to make sure you’re doing a good job. And I think that is the real challenge for them.We’ve been at it for about 45 minutes. I still don’t know how David Ellison is gonna make one more dollar than he made last year. Have you come to any conclusions?We’re recording this Tuesday morning. Tuesday night, like at 7:30? I don’t know why they’re doing it at 7:30 or 8:30. They’re gonna have a press conference, the first Skydance press conference. So if we re-record this on Wednesday, maybe all this will be answered, but maybe it won’t be answered.Well, Ynon will be there. He’ll be there wielding his scythe.It’s gonna be interesting because he is not gonna be a high-profile person, but I think a lot of people are gonna learn his name anyway. And this is a thing that Hollywood does, right? You find a person to blame for your troubles. Sometimes it’s a company like Netflix, sometimes it’s an evil Jason Kilar. Remember when he was running WarnerMedia for a minute or two? And everyone said, “You’re wrecking the business. Thank God we have David Zaslav, who’s an authentic media guy to come in and save us.” And then, you know, six months later, David Zaslav’s name is an epithet. Presumably there’ll be a new epithet associated with this company.Yeah. Well, this deal is gonna wind its way through. We’re gonna check in on it a lot. We’re gonna have you back, Peter. Thank you so much for being on

item.title: Things from the Aaron Boone era that I’m sick of watching
item.author: Matt Ferenchick
item.content:encoded: This year’s ALDS sweep at the hands of the Rays felt like a culmination for the Aaron Boone era Yankees. I’m not sure it will be a culmination of his managerial tenure as I could definitely see the team keeping him, but those three games felt like everything that has gone wrong in a Yankees’ playoff exit from 2018 to now all rolled into one. There were mental mistakes, sloppy play, and bats going cold all at once.I think it would be unfair to say that Boone hasn’t grown at all since taking the job. Early in his tenure, I used to get frustrated by him sticking with a pitcher too long trying to steal an extra out or two. These days, it seems pretty rare that those instances happen. However, any growth from him is overshadowed by the frustration that I share with many other Yankee fans.In watching this year’s playoff defeat, my mind couldn’t help but keep going over the things that went wrong that I could see coming, because all of Boone’s teams seem to suffer in these ways. Whether or not the Yankees do bring Aaron Boone back, I personally am out, and it would take a massive change of fortune to change that. Here are the reasons why.For one, his teams seem to play with just no sense of fundamentals. I am an analytically-inclined fan, so when I say this, I don’t meant that they don’t bunt enough or that they need to learn to go the other way and hit singles, because I think there are logical reasons that make it easier said than done against the pitchers of today. However, there are some baseball things that happen in the heat of the moment of a game that don’t make sense no matter your way of thinking.Austin Wells getting thrown out try to stretch a double into a triple in Game 1 of the ALDS is the perfect example. “Don’t make the last out of the inning at third base” is a longtime baseball axiom that makes perfect sense. With two outs, you can’t score on a sacrifice fly or any other kind of productive out, so those 90 feet matter way less than just having a chance with a runner in scoring position. Yet in the heat of the game, Wells seemingly wasn’t even thinking about that, never mind the fact that he ran through Luis Rojas’ stop sign too.I feel like I regularly watch the Yankees allow opposing runners to take extra bases because a fielder tries for an out at home that has like a five percent chance at happening rather than throwing ahead of the runner, holding them, and living to fight for another day. Or, an infielder will try and make a rushed and/or spectacular throw to try and complete a double play leading to an error, and a runner getting an extra base (à la Jazz Chisholm Jr. in Game 2). I know it’s probably hard to think about these things in the moment and your instincts will kick in to some degree, but it feels like the Yankees regularly disadvantage themselves by going to the spectacular instead of sticking to basics.Relatededly, I have another issue with the defense in general. Anthony Volpe went from winning a Gold Glove as a rookie to looking like a shortstop novice in just two seasons. It’s cost the Yankees some playoff games, including the infamous 2024 World Series Game 5 meltdown. Again, errors are something that are going to occur no matter what, but the Boone Yankees have been so sloppy so often.That sloppiness also almost always comes to a head during an almost annual mid-season — usually around June or July — swoon.Another baseball saying is that every team wins 50 and loses 50, and your season is decided by what you do in the rest of the games. For the most part, that holds true and I don’t think there’s any manager who could’ve snapped their fingers and won 110 games with any of Boone’s Yankees teams. Every team is going to slump. However, why is it that every Boone team will start off hot and then go through about a month where they appear to forget how to play baseball?This year, they went 12-14 in June. If you expand that out to a couple days either side of the month, they had a 15-20 stretch. In 2025, they were under .500 in all of June and July. They were under .500 in July 2024, and that includes a five-game winning streak at the end of the month. They were on pace for 122 wins in mid-June 2022 and ended up winning under 100.Again, I recognize that every team is going to have some slumps. The MLB-best Brewers were just barely over .500 after April and ended up with 103 wins. No team is going to put up exactly even .600 winning percentages every month — even the 1998 Yankees played a few ticks below that pace in September. However, I would appreciate if the Yankees stop having a stretch that obviously foreshadows what is going to happen that October.Another issue that has played out in the postseason, but sometimes appears in the regular season as well is that the Boone Yankees’ teams never get the last laugh. I don’t mean this just in a “they haven’t won the World Series” sense, but they always seem to be the team that ends with with egg on their face.In 2020, they got into it with the Rays after Aroldis Chapman airmailed a pitch over Mike Brosseau’s head, leading to a verbal back and forth between the two teams, on the field and in the media. What happens that October? The Yankees lose to the Rays after … Mike Brosseau homers off Aroldis Chapman.In a 2021 Subway Series game, Francisco Lindor made allusions to what he perceived as the Yankees’ stealing signs. Giancarlo Stanton chirped him back after he hit a home run, leading to the benches clearing. However, what ended up deciding the game? Lindor’s third homer of the game.Beyond just losing every postseason under Boone, the Yankees constantly end up the butt of jokes, and frankly I’m done with it.

item.title: On the Yankees’ playoff failures and the agony of apathy
item.author: Joshua Diemert
item.content:encoded: I try very hard to fight back against apathy. In politics, the economy, media, the world begs for your apathy. Don’t make a fuss, let it all just happen. It’s all going According to Plan. The state apparatus depends on your apathy. Do not give them that gift.And yet, not quite 48 hours after the Yankees once again lost in the ALDS, lost to a team seeded higher than them, lost to a team that is just so fundamentally annoying that thinking about them raises my blood pressure a point or two…I don’t feel much at all.I’ve always tried to hedge my reactions to bad sports news. The Don LeGreca-style rants make for good radio and some of the longer, more unhinged comments we get here are fun to scroll past, but at the end of the day I consume baseball for my own entertainment. Letting yourself get mad over something you say you enjoy while having 0 control over it hasn’t made a whole lot of sense to me. Let sports lift you up, not press you down.And true to form, I’m not mad about the 2026 Yankees. I’m beige. The Yankees dogwalked the Red Sox last week only to find themselves canine-ized by the Rays, swept out of the ALDS in what’s actually a worse result than last year. (They lasted a whole four games against the Blue Jays!) Aaron Boone put the worst leadoff hitter in baseball atop the lineup, telling us that he liked the potential for action on the basepaths ahead of the only batter who showed up in the series, and that leadoff hitter went 0-for-5 as the team died—with him as the final out—because of course he did.I don’t quite know why I’m so numb to all of this. The Yankees won 93 games, the second-best record in the AL, without the game’s best player, while actively rehabbing three pitchers in their starting rotation, while Austin Wells was locked in the trunk of a car for four months, while shortstop was an open question until the season’s final few weeks. It should be kind of remarkable that they were even in the dance in the first place?But the AL was so bad, the table so uncompetitive, that the Yankees didn’t really outrun the other guy being chased by the bear. There was no bear at all. The team wasn’t good enough to chase down the Rays, dooming themselves to an additional two playoff games while the Rays got to rest, prepare, and welcome the Yankees to the Trop for the start of the series. The same offense we’d seen sleepwalk through the year for weeks at a time showed themselves, they lost, and I don’t really care.Supposedly at the staff level the organization is starting to pick at itself like an under-stimulated pet bird. This annual tradition of “just be good enough to make it before 26 people who should be among the best in the world at what they do collectively forget what their jobs are” might finally be sinking in. At the top level though we’ll be told not to worry, There is A Plan, these guys are having good at bats actually, it’s right in front of us.Congratulations to the New York Yankees. You’ve managed to accomplish something my government and AI companies haven’t. Sure, man, whatever you say, I shrug my shoulders and I walk down the street.

item.title: Winners and losers from F1's wet Singapore GP sprint race
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: But that still demanded cool heads of the 22 drivers - some of whom were more successful at keeping cool than others.Here's our pick of winners and losers from the sixth and final sprint race of the 2026 Formula 1 season.“I just misjudged it,” George Russell said of his early race-ending Singapore crash.Even if this is likely to make no difference to his ever-dwindling title hopes, Russell is in a position where, for his own sake, he needs to end the year on a high.Grabbing the lead from Verstappen at the start in the sprint looked like the perfect way to do that before a grid penalty hobbles the rest of his weekend.But the heavy crash - which he put down to having more power than expected from the battery exiting the final corner and then touching the white line as he ran a little wide - put paid to that in a very painful way.“It's a very, very silly mistake,” he said. “Overly confident. Think it's my first crash of the year. It's annoying to happen from that position.”Winner: Kimi Antonelli (4th)This was a quintessential ‘when it’s your year, it’s your year’ kind of day for Kimi Antonelli.He did nothing remarkable - which in itself is good because evidently these were conditions it was easy to trip up in - and yet took another little step towards his world championship.His chief title ‘rival’ Russell crashed out of a winning position on the first lap. Then, at the very end, two cars ahead of him were removed by a needless collision.Apart from keeping the car on the road this is the easiest progress Antonelli will make all season - and it almost ended in an unlikely sprint podium, such was Leclerc’s trouble by the end of the race.Loser: McLaren (8th & 14th)A frustrating but solid race turned into a needlessly destructive one for McLaren thanks to Lando Norris’s over-ambitious final lap move.Sending it down the inside of Turn 5 in the wet is borderline desperate at the best of times, let alone against your team-mate.McLaren chiefs must have been holding their breath when it happened but ultimately, while gutted, surely not surprised that it caused a synchronised pirouette from the pair, ending Oscar Piastri’s race in the process.It was always likely to end badly and it could yet get worse if Norris cops a penalty for it that loses him eighth place, and with it the measly point McLaren still got as a weak silver lining.Winner: Max Verstappen (1st)Would Verstappen have had anything to come back at Russell with? We'll never know - though you could infer that Verstappen might've found it difficult considering his assertion post-race that "I think we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass".That's all academic. Verstappen never looked under threat from behind, and his drive to victory had an air of cruise control to it - at a track, too, where Verstappen can struggle to reach his peak level of performance.Yet more evidence that the four-time champion is the form driver right now.Loser: Isack Hadjar (DNF)It's hard to judge Hadjar too harshly considering he managed only two laps before parking up with a power issue.But he did lose two places at the start, if we're being ultra-critical.And of course, there's no escaping the fact this was a DNF in a race won by the sister car.Winner: Lewis Hamilton (2nd)Lewis Hamilton did the hard work for his sprint race in the opening few seconds, leaping forward past his team-mate and the two McLarens.Considering he seemed to have the best pace of anyone besides Verstappen in this race, that was critical. Getting stuck on a track where it looked almost impossible to overtake in these conditions - barring bigger pace swings in the midfield - would have made Hamilton’s sprint look a lot more average.He couldn't quite match Verstappen in the middle of the race but started to whittle away at the lead again late on and was much, much better managing his tyres than team-mate Leclerc seemed to be as the track dried.Winner: Liam Lawson (5th)If you can keep your head when all around you are losing theirs...OK, the Singapore sprint wasn't the most difficult to navigate in reality, but there was still plenty of reward to be reaped from keeping it neat and tidy.This was another exemplary drive from Lawson, who in repeating his best-of-the-rest trick from qualifying also stood to gain from any incidents up ahead. (Hello, McLaren.)It's this sort of drive that means the direction of travel is only going one way in the fight for fifth in the constructors' championship between Racing Bulls and Alpine right now.Loser: Arvid Lindblad (13th)Compare Lawson's serene run to fifth with Racing Bulls team-mate Lindblad's travails.Lindblad was perplexed after the race by his spin under the safety car - "it was a bit confusing at the time because it was pretty gentle on power, then just suddenly lost it" - but was a little loose in his description of events that "then I tried to just get it back round", as he in fact had spent multiple seconds driving the car backwards while trying to loop around at Turn 5.No surprise then that that caught the attention of race control.And even if he escapes penalty, this was a last-on-the-road finish in the same car that finished well up the road in fifth. There's no question, considering the attrition, that points were up for grabs.Loser: Cadillac (DNF & DNF)Two cars. Two collisions. One unproductive race.The Sergio Perez-Lance Stroll clash looked like as clear a case of racing incident as you'll find, so there's little blame to be apportioned to the Cadillac driver there.Valtteri Bottas doesn't get such an easy ride. What initially looked like a lazy slide from Alex Albon into the back of Gabriel Bortoleto was actually the result of Bottas getting into the back of the Williams. All this before the race had restarted, too.The "rubber band" effect was partly to blame - Bottas said "the two cars ahead of me came to full stop and I just didn't have time to react" - but he did ultimately trigger contact.So much for this being the sort of weekend, and track, that can play into Cadillac's hands...Winner: Ollie Bearman (6th)Ollie Bearman was absolutely thrilled with his work in the sprint, even though he acknowledged his seven-place rise was bolstered by others screwing up.Irrespective of the Russell shunt and McLaren collision, though, Bearman was a man on the move here. He toughed it out nicely to get ahead of Pierre Gasly once the race resumed post-safety car, and that was critical for consolidating a points finish.Bearman was on course to grab eighth irrespective of what happened on the final lap - so the bump up to sixth merely boosted the Haas driver rather than flattered his efforts completely.

item.content:encoded: Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenicThe US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review.The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb).Continue reading...

item.title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean
item.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
item.content:encoded: Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equalityThey were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In the Peterloo massacre of 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.A study by Global Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – as Robert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.Continue reading...

item.title: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
item.author: Jacek Krywko
item.content:encoded: For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.

item.title: Tourism expansion v turtle nests: the dispute dividing communities in one Tobago resort
item.author: Jewel Fraser in Rocky Point, Tobago
item.content:encoded: Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitatVisitors to Rocky Point in south-west Tobago are drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest.But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best.Continue reading...

item.title: Three winners and three losers from Knicks’ first two preseason games
item.author: Kento Kato
item.content:encoded: The Knicks are back to playing basketball and are less than two weeks away from opening night. They’ve started 0-2, which nobody really cares about, but we’ve also now seen enough minutes from the exhibition matches to get a glimpse of who the winners and losers have been in the early portion of the preseason.Winner: Jalen Brunson and his wristShould anyone have really doubted or even been remotely worried about Brunson’s offseason wrist surgery? No, the captain has repeatedly been the definition of reliable. So it was ridiculous to ever think that Brunson wouldn’t be prepared or would look off coming off of his injury. But fans are unreasonable. And also, he is a 30 year-old who had an operation on his shooting hand. Fortunately for Knicks fans, though, he’s looked as good as any other Knicks. His three-point shot was off against the Wizards as he went just 1-for-6. But Brunson looks like he’s in midseason form. He’s taking his usual shots, which include, but aren’t limited to, driving layups, floaters, mid-range fadeaways, and pull-up threes, and he’s looked comfortable and confident in doing so. Defensively, he’s started the preseason giving good effort, and he’s already drawn multiple charges as well. Brunson and his wrist seem to be doing just fine.Loser: Pacome Dadiet and his trade valueComing into training camp and preseason, there couldn’t have been many expectations for Dadiet. He’s now had two full seasons of pretty much being non-existent. His Summer League left a lot to be desired. And he played worse than most fans could’ve imagined during the World Cup qualifiers for the Ivory Coast team. Yet even after all that, he’s found a way to disappoint so far in preseason. In the preseason opener, the team was clearly trying to give him an opportunity to either increase his trade value or at least win some spot minutes, and he failed to do that. And he wasn’t much better in game two against the Wizards.It’s only been two games, but they’ve both been a failure for Dadiet. He’s scored just nine total points in 30 minutes of play and is shooting just 28.6% from the field without standing out as a playmaker, rebounder, or defender. Dadiet’s path to being a rotation player in New York was pretty thin to begin with. But whatever opportunity he had to at least help the team out by increasing his trade value may be slipping away now too. Shamet is coming off of two straight training camps where his job wasn’t even guaranteed. He’s battled back from injuries and has consistently displayed a perfect balance of selflessness and staying ready. That led to him becoming an integral part of the Knicks’ rotation last year. And he was rewarded with a very nice four-year, $24 million contract. Shamet rewarded the Knicks and their loyalty by reportedly turning down offers from other contenders.Now back with the same team for the third straight year-something he’s never done before in his career-the journeyman looks comfortable and confident. He looks poised to not just continue what he’s done but build upon it and has gotten off to an extremely hot start in preseason. He’s averaging 11.5PPG in just 13.5MPG and is shooting an extremely hot 53.3% from the field and 50% from three.The talk around McBride for much of the offseason has been about what the Knicks could get in a trade for him. And after the offensive struggles he went through in the Finals, there are some fans who may have forgotten just how good and valuable the reserve guard is. He’s still one of the best bench perimeter defenders in the league, and that, combined with his much improved three-point shooting, makes him so pivotal to what Mike Brown and the Knicks want to do. And nobody should be overly concerned about what he does or doesn’t do in the preseason.That being said, he’s currently struggling mightily offensively. McBride has so far averaged just 3PPG on 18.2% shooting from the field and 11.1% shooting from three. There were some expectations that he’d showcase a little more after a full offseason to work on some of his weaknesses that got exposed against the Spurs. And fans were excited to see him fully healthy after he revealed that he was still hurt throughout the postseason run. He should be fine eventually, but it’s been a rough go for McBride so far.Many fans had different reactions when Drummond signed with the Knicks this past summer. Some were excited, some were indifferent, and some were disappointed. New York still has a very long season ahead of them, and that should come with opportunities to upgrade at this position one way or another. And during said long season, Drummond will inevitably go through ups and downs. But so far, the veteran center has looked solid. His pick-and-roll defense, something many were concerned about, has actually looked good. He’s been very active with his hands, and his defense there, especially when paired up with the also active Jose Alvarado, could be a fun tandem. Drummond’s finishing ability is concerning due to his lack of explosiveness. But his surprisingly solid defense, along with his elite-as-advertised rebounding, has been fun to watch. Losers: Drew Eubanks, Ochai Agbaji, and Tony BradleyBruce Brown Jr. was looked at as one of the favorites to win the Knicks’ last roster spot given the team’s previous interest in him. Other than that, there really wasn’t a consensus. Some wanted James Wiseman for his potential. Others wanted Eubanks for his defense, passing, and experience. Others wanted Agbaji for… not really sure why.Two games into preseason, it looks clear who Brown and the Knicks have the most interest in. Brown, Wiseman, and Jaden Akins are the only three of the training camp invitees to play in both games. On Thursday night against the Wizards, Eubanks, Agbaji, and Bradley were DNPs. Now, this may just be the way they are splitting up the minutes, and maybe those guys see minutes over Brown and Wiseman when they play the Timberwolves on Monday. Brown, although not overly impressive, has looked solid. And Wiseman, especially against the 76ers, looked good. Neither is locked in to make the roster just yet. But it seems like they are a head above Eubanks, Agbaji, and Bradley.

item.title: Bauke Mollema, Pello Bilbao and other retiring riders receive guard of honour send-off at Il Lombardia
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: The retiring riders for whom Il Lombardia will be their final race received a warm send-off and a guard of honour from the peloton at the start of the Italian Monument in Bergamo on Saturday morning.Multiple riders are closing the curtain on their careers in Italy this Saturday, including former winner Bauke Mollema (Lidl-Trek), plus Pello Bilbao (Bahrain Victorious), Rudy Molard (Groupama-FDJ United), Odd Christian Eiking (Unibet Rose Rockets) and Ion Izagirre (Cofidis).At the start, the retirees were presented with a guard of honour from their peloton colleagues, who lined the road with their bikes in the air to wave off the departing riders. Mollema, who won this race in 2019 and has the most starts in the current peloton with a whopping 17, was also presented with a medal and framed plaque on stage during the team sign-on to commemorate the last race of his career.This comes alongside a special Netherlands-themed paint job on his Trek bike for his final race."There's quite a lot going through my mind today, it's a special day, ending my career here in Lombardia, in a race that I won and that has given me a lot," the Dutchman told at the start. "It's been a long journey, almost 20 years in professional cycling, and today is the last day, in a race I love. I've always loved to race in Italy, so I hope to enjoy it a bit, but it will also be a lot of suffering."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Verstappen wins delayed Singapore sprint, Russell crashes from lead
item.author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
item.content:encoded: Max Verstappen won an attritional Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix sprint race bookended by initial race leader George Russell crashing out and the two McLarens colliding.After a delayed start due to heavy rain in the build-up to the sprint, Russell jumped Verstappen into the first corner - but his lead barely lasted a full lap.The Mercedes driver, for whom a win might have barely kept alive his faint title hopes, spun exiting the final corner and crashed into the pitwall just beyond the timing line.That freed up Verstappen to take a controlled victory (after a safety car period) in which he steadily built his lead over Lewis Hamilton and managed it easily until the end.Hamilton’s second place was earned from a lightning start that vaulted him ahead of both McLarens and his Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc.And he was clearly the faster Ferrari in these conditions as Leclerc faded extremely badly late on, putting him under pressure from Oscar Piastri, Lando Norris and a muted championship leader Kimi Antonelli.Leclerc looked to have done enough to stave off the McLaren threat even before they collided calamitously on the final lap.Norris launched a silly move on his team-mate into the Turn 5 right-hander. Piastri left some room on the inside but Norris, who went over the kerb, hit his team-mate's car and spun both of them round.Though Norris rejoined after a short delay and claimed a point in eighth - a point he may lose given the incident is under investigation - Piastri retired in the wall.This gifted Antonelli fourth and elevated several midfield cars into healthy points positions.Liam Lawson spearheaded this group with a very accomplished drive to fifth while Ollie Bearman was sixth for Haas - keeping Nico Hulkenberg from his team’s championship rival Audi at bay in the process.Hulkenberg had robustly passed Pierre Gasly earlier in the race to run behind Bearman but looked set to end the sprint empty-handed before McLaren imploded.Among the nine retirees were also Isack Hadjar and Franco Colapinto, who suffered stoppages during the early safety car period, first-lap colliders Lance Stroll and Sergio Perez, and Alex Albon, Gabriel Bortoleto and Valtteri Bottas.Albon and Bortoleto collided ahead of the safety car period ending in an incident that will be investigated after the race.

item.title: 'I just had nothing to lose' – Tiffany Cromwell delivers feisty farewell in Nannup at home UCI Gravel World Championships
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: The Australian rider has won at the SEVEN Gravel World Series race held in the same location three times, and she was going to make the most of that home advantage to time her moves."When you know it's your last one, the head space was good. I knew I just had nothing to lose," Cromwell told after crossing her final finish line.The outcome was eighth as she took on her fifth and final Gravel Worlds, but she carved out a spectacular path along the way. The first key selection, as expected, was made on Brockman and Cromwell became part of the chase group, which through the next section just kept chipping away at the gap. Cromwell finally closed the last bit and rather than sitting in, decided she may as well just keep on going. "In gravel, I've always been good at just getting in my rhythm, and I think just the dynamic at the front – nobody really wants to show their cards too quickly – it seemed to play into my favour." Initially it looked like Cromwell's move would be short-lived, with Marianne Vos (Netherlands) among those to go out in pursuit, but then her rivals started looking at each other and the gap stretched, sitting at over a minute at 70km to go in the 125.6km race with 3,179m of elevation gain."It was obviously early on but It was like 'OK, you know, why not try something, get a head start," she said, who knew that she "always suffered" on the Ellis climb ahead."Getting that far and having the head start was perfect because then it put me really back in the game."I knew I couldn't match the girls on the climb, so I just had to take a chance, and I think it was just one of those days, you're just not thinking, you're not doubting yourself."So even though she was caught, dropped and then clawed her way back again once more it was Cromwell who was charging into the brutal climb of Folly with just under 30km to go, delivering an excited roar and chatter from among the waiting crowd who hadn't been expecting her to be on the charge, or perhaps even in the lead group, once again."I was like, 'I'm cooked, I could sit here, get dropped in a few k or attack," she said. "And the way gravel works, a lot of individual riders against each other, nobody wants to necessarily chase straight away, so again, it just gave me another head start for Folly. But then I was like, done, done."Though she still held on for a finish within the top ten, even sprinting to the line against Elisa Serné (Netherlands) to make sure she got eight and not ninth. "I wanted to come here, race my bike, give everything I had, and just be at the finish having no regrets," concluded Cromwell as she did her final round of post-race media interviews to conclude a career spanning 17 seasons, and with a bank of many successes – which now includes her second UCI Gravel World Championships top 10.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Sprint start crash causes huge tension within Aprilia
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Raul Fernandez has repeatedly excoriated Aprilia stablemate Marco Bezzecchi for his role in setting up their crash at the start of the Mandalika sprint, describing Bezzecchi's tactics as "not nice", "ungentlemanly" and "not clever".Fernandez fractured his left index finger in the crash at the start of the sprint, which was triggered as four riders - Fernandez, Bezzecchi, Marc Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio - went into Turn 1 almost side-by-side and their lines converged deep into the corner.As Di Giannantonio ran Marquez out wide, Bezzecchi checked up and had contact with Fernandez that took both out of the race and injured the latter. Fernandez is now in doubt for the grand prix, but will try to contest the warm-up.Fernandez was seething after the sprint, giving explosive interviews to both Spanish broadcaster DAZN and Italian broadcaster Sky Sport, in which he effectively accused Bezzecchi of deliberately compromising his race at the cost of letting two Ducatis through.His tone softened between the TV interviews and the written media, but his argument remained the same. Bezzecchi, he felt, approached Turn 1 with the focus only on beating Fernandez, squeezed him out and left the door open for the two Ducatis, which created the conditions for the crash."For me, the crash is a consequence of the start," Fernandez said. "On the start, for me I tried to keep my bike in the middle of the track, to try to not open the door for other riders to overtake. Marco had made a really good start and he overtook me - he didn't really overtake 100 percent, but he put the bike close to me and started to take me out the track. "And this is for me the more frustrating thing about today. When you want to do something that is not clean in this sport. We are riders, we put our body [on the line] at more than 300km/h and when you are doing something that you know that is not really nice, I am not happy with that. "And for me the version is, OK, we crash, it doesn't matter, it can happen, one day it will be me that I will make a mistake, another day will be another rider. The problem is when you are making something that you know is not nice. And for me this is the big problem that we saw today. "We go out [wide] he doesn't give me space, two Ducatis overtook us, we crash, that's it."Fernandez chuckled that it was "for sure not good" as a strategy by Bezzecchi. He said the Aprilia riders knew the battle for victory would play out between them, and accused Bezzecchi of "thinking just of me"."I am not playing for the championship. He was playing for the championship. For me he was not very smart."He also indicated he was more upset with Bezzecchi over this than with Jorge Martin over the Balaton Park pile-up at Turn 1, as that had been a mere mistake and this was a premeditated "bad action to another rider".He said it was nothing that could or should be penalised but that Bezzecchi "didn't have the respect" and that, while Aprilia riders are told to be "gentlemen" with one another in terms of wheel-to-wheel racing, it "looks like he [Bezzecchi] was not a gentleman with us".Bezzecchi defends himselfBezzecchi was told of Fernandez's incandescence but chalked it up to heat-of-the-moment emotions clouding Fernandez's judgment. "I am maybe the one who can confirm this more than anyone," he joked, in seeming reference to his ban at Assen for striking a marshal.It was a "racing incident", Bezzecchi insisted. "I was just looking to put myself in the best place possible for the braking. I knew Marc could try to overtake but was for me useless to try to force too much and maybe throw away the race in the first corner. "It's what I did. If Raul is angry, I'm sorry, but honestly, he touched me! So at the end there's nothing to be angry for. Me versus him or him versus me, at the end it was a racing incident. I couldn't disappear and he also couldn't disappear. I don't want to waste energy with this, I want to focus for tomorrow."How the Ducati pair saw itMarquez, who went on to win the sprint, said the incident was "easy to explain"."Four bikes in parallel, and I believe that Bezzecchi was looking at Raul, to brake a bit later, I was looking at Bezzecchi to brake a bit later, and Diggia was looking at me to brake a bit later. The consequence - four riders out of the line and [Jorge] Martin from fifth to first," he recounted.Di Giannantonio had been completely unaware that anyone had crashed - but did say that contact with Marquez coming through the corner caused a downshift on his end that then compromised his exit from Turn 1."Honestly, you have to ask the others [about the incident] - me, I just got hit again."

item.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 10/10/26
item.author: Jake Devin
item.content:encoded: It’s Day 3 of a post-2026 Yankees world, and the MLB playoffs continue on without the Bombers. Tonight, the Rays will learn who they’ll be playing in the ALCS on Monday at Tropicana Field, as the 2-0 advantage that the White Sox once held vanished upon their return to the South Side. The Guardians won both games in Chicago and can complete the 2001 Yankees-esque comeback with just one win tonight back home in Cleveland. No matter who emerges, they will be heavy underdogs against the top-seeded Rays.On the site today, Josh discusses the apathy he, and surely many other fans, are feeling after another Yankees exit that felt just so typical. Later, John writes up David Bednar for our Yankees Birthday series, while Kento analyzes Aaron Boone’s perplexing decision to bat Trent Grisham leadoff in Game 3, and Matt offers his biggest gripes with the Boone Era. With the NLCS already set and beginning tomorrow night, Peter also previews that Dodgers/Brewers rematch, which Milwaukee is hoping is a closer than the 2025 version.American League Division Series Game 5Cleveland Guardians vs. Chicago White Sox(RHP Gavin Williams vs. RHP Sean Burke)TV: TBS/HBO Max, TruTV, UnivisionVenue: Progressive Field, Cleveland, OH1. Will any of the Yankees significant pending free agents (David Bednar, Trent Grisham, Paul Blackburn, Jazz Chisholm Jr.) be back with the team next year?2. Does tonight’s Game 5 between the Guardians and White Sox intrigue you? Or are you left feeling empty, both because of the Yankees’ exit from the postseason, and the underwhelming quality of both these AL Central squads?

item.title: 'At the end of the day, you can only try' – Despite puncture and a late crash, Rosa Klöser claws back silver at UCI Gravel World Championships
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: It was just 20km into the UCI Gravel World Championships elite women's race on Saturday and Rosa Klöser (Germany) thought it may have already been over, when a tricky flat dropped her out of the lead group not long before the first crucial climb of the day.But somehow, some 100km later, she was out front with Marianne Vos (Netherlands) and contending for the win."It was definitely a tough race. I mean, the course is really relentless," Klöser told after going to the podium to claim her silver medal. The bad luck also seemed to be just as relentless for the rider wearing the number 13 on her back, as it turned out her flat tyre wouldn't be the only misfortune of her day."It was a really big job for me to come back because it was also not easy to find the hole in my tyre, so it took me really quite a while until I got going again," said Klöser. "And if I'm honest, I saw the race move away from me there, but I was like, 'OK, you know what, you can only try'. So I kept pushing, and when I could see them I got an extra gear and I managed to come back to the front group,"The front group ebbed and flowed as groups rejoined and then were again shed on the unrelenting course and a caught stick caused another quick stop for Klöser , that, however was quickly dealt with and the Canyon-SRAM-MAAP rider went with Vos at around 20km to go Once she made it, however, her travails weren't over, with a stick caught in her rear mech, but that barely made a dent compared to the other chase back which could well have weakened her sprint. Klöser, who has also spent a considerable amount of time on the road this year, jumped back into gravel with a couple of UCI Gravel World Series races in September, winning both and in one of them, Sea Otter Europe, shaking off Vos. It's clear that Klöser was coming into the race with a course that seemed to suit her and some powerful form. "I won't lie, it was a really big goal," said Kloser, who did have her season interrupted by a parasitic infection that she was unaware of, but worked it out in time to prepare for the rainbow jersey race.As the final 10km approached, it looked set to come down to a sprint battle between Vos, who is renowned for her prowess in delivering a sprint finish at the end of a tough race, and Klöser, who managed to pull off a huge gravel win when she clinched Unbound in a sprint of nine. But more bad luck struck before Klöser could even think about the sprint."Unfortunately, I think with 4km to go, I wiped out in like the last technical corner," said the rider who fronted up for the podium ceremonies and post-race interviews with a ripped shorts, a wound on one leg and a banged-up arm. "I probably overinflated my tyre also a bit when when it got flat. But I mean that's racing, that's gravel. At the end of the day, you can only try."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Why Martin had to give up MotoGP sprint win
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: MotoGP's former championship leader Jorge Martin had to surrender the Mandalika sprint win and points lead due to the risk of a tyre pressure infringement.After an opening-corner melee removed fellow Aprilia riders Raul Fernandez and Marco Bezzecchi from the picture, and gave Martin 'free' passage into first from fifth on the grid, the Aprilia man looked to be in control and en route to a comfortable victory.But Martin suddenly slowed and allowed title rival Marc Marquez through, in a move that looked like a bid to get some heat onto his front tyre and avoid a ruinous eight-second penalty for non-compliance.The front tyre must be kept above the baseline pressure - around 1.8 bar, though it varies slightly from round to round - for at least 30% of the total laps in the sprint - and Martin confirmed after the race that this was indeed the reason why he had to abandon the lead.His attempts to then strike back on Marquez came to naught, and a mistake on the penultimate lap dropped him to fourth place - turning what was set to be a five-point lead over Marquez exiting the race into a four-point deficit."I didn't do a great start but they were four[-wide] into first corner so it was easy for me to go into the lead," Martin recounted. "Then I tried to push and I was able to make a big gap to Marc. But then I realised that I was under the pressure [requirement]. I tried to push the front more, tried to warm it a bit more, but it wasn't into the [legal] zone. "So I had to let Marc past, and then after that everything started to get a bit difficult. Even if I was trying to be close [to Marquez] to make a move into the last lap - that's why I made a mistake with two laps to go, and then the chances were gone."Martin felt that he still carried a "big opportunity" into Sunday to re-assert himself in the championship race."For sure tomorrow Marco [Bezzecchi] and [Raul] Fernandez will be super strong - but so will I," he said, albeit perhaps unaware that Fernandez is believed to have sustained a hand injury in the Turn 1 crash.Why was the pressure too low?Martin and his crew chief Daniele Romagnoli may not have expected to lead the race - given he was fifth on the grid, and didn't necessarily have the pace to easily clear his fellow Aprilias.But Martin insisted they didn't set the front tyre pressure particularly low in the expectation of running in the pack."It's not a thing that we normally do. We never risk with the tyre pressure, I don't know why today we were out [of the limit]."I think here it's quite difficult with the humidity, and maybe it changed from yesterday. But honestly we didn't risk. "Sometimes it happens. It hasn't happened to me a lot in the last few years, but today [it has]. So for sure it's something we need to check, because it's something that today maybe 0.1 [bar higher] I was able to win the same and not be in trouble."

item.title: 'We cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying' –Riders stage remarkable protest at Il Lombardia as Evenepoel delivers speech on safety
item.author: Matilda Price
item.content:encoded: There were remarkable scenes at the start of Il Lombardia on Saturday morning, as the peloton staged a protest and refused to start the race for a full five minutes. Even more remarkably, Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) grabbed a microphone and delivered a speech, explaining to the race organisers and the general public that the riders were making a statement over rider safety.Suspicions that some sort of protest might be brewing were raised when Evenepoel, Tom Pidcock (Pinarello-Q36.5) and Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek) approached the senior race officials on the start line, a few minutes prior to the start of the race.It would appear there was no more forewarning than that, as the race’s official master of ceremonies began the countdown from 10 seconds to the race start, only for the riders to remain unmoved when the start of the race was signalled.After around two minutes, in which the race speaker declared "some sort of delay", Evenepoel was handed a microphone and addressed the gathered public in the centre of Bergamo."I will speak in English in the name of the whole bunch and not only the guys who are here but everyone in pro cycling," he said."We want to make this statement because there's too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race. Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world that we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or literally dying in what we like the most to do," he said, making reference to the death of Finlay Tarling."So this is why we want to spend five minutes more still to make our statement towards organisations, to the public, to everybody that is following cycling, because we cannot accept the fact that people are dying. This is why we stand still, we pay our tribute and respect to all the riders who are already involved in incidents."To the organisers who organise races in the future, please make sure that we can race safely, and that we can just do what we like to do without being worried about cars, motorbikes, all that stuff, coming into the course."Evenepoel's speech was met with applause from the spectators and his fellow riders.'We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act'Tom Pidcock, whose teammates were involved in the incident at Tre Valli Varesine – and admitted he nearly stopped riding then – has been vocal about the issue of safety, and posted a statement to his Instagram to coincide with the protest. Various other riders posted the same joint statement."As riders, we stand united against the unnecessary risk our lives are being subjected to," it read."This week alone, there were multiple incidents of vehicles on race courses. Two riders crashed when they hit a motorbike who was driving the wrong way on the race route. Luckily both escaped with cuts and bruises, it could have been so much worse. "This summer, a life was tragically lost to exactly this kind of failure. We will not stand for this any longer. Riders race at high speed with little protection, and we depend on the UCI and race organisers to secure the roads. That responsibility is not being met. "We are calling for the UCI and race organisers to take accountability and act. That means a serious, open conversation between riders, race organisers and the UCI resulting in concrete changes to how race routes are secured and managed. "After five minutes, we raced as normal. We did not want to affect the race, only to show what riders can do when we stand as one. We love this sport. We respect the race organisers. We want to race hard and put on a show for our fans. However most importantly we want to come home safe to our loved ones."CPA president Adam Hansen shared the same statement on his Twitter account on Saturday morning.After around five minutes of standstill, the flag was dropped for a second time and the peloton rolled out for the neutralised start.RCS, who organise Il Lombardia but not any of the earlier Italian races where incidents have occurred, voiced their support for the protest, though without mentioning the demand for race organisers to act."At the start of Il Lombardia presented by Crédit Agricole, the riders came together to send an important message, stopping for five minutes to urge all road users to behave responsibly and show mutual respect, both during races and in everyday life," a release from the organisers read. "RCS Sport fully supports this appeal, aimed at ensuring everyone's safety."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia.
