item.title: 'I would love to see an actual gravel rider winning the jersey' – An established gravel incarnation of Nicole Frain lines up as key hope for home-nation at Nannup Gravel World Championships
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: This is the third UCI Gravel World Championships for Australia's Nicole Frain, and she has been steadily working her way up the ranks, while also plotting out such a solid path in the discipline that it's easy to forget it's only her second season focused completely on gravel.Back in 2024, when she first lined up at the rainbow jersey race, Frain had been racing on the road for Hess, though the team collapsed late in the season. However, she'd already been racing gravel at times in 2024, with strong results that included a run of seconds in RADL GRVL and the UCI Gravel World Series races of The Gralloch and Houffa and then her first World Championships in Belgium, where Marianne Vos won. "I think the first year I definitely went in with no expectations, and then I surprised myself getting into a really good position. I had stomach issues, but at least for the race, I did put myself into a really good position if it all came together," said Frain who came over the line in 33rd.Then in 2025 gravel became the main focus for the former Australian road champion, joining the Ridley team, throwing herself into the UCI Gravel World Series and honing her skills. Impressively she also took the overall victory at the series, which meant a start at the front of the field both packed with and dominated by Dutch riders."Last year, I learnt about the dynamic," Frain told in the weeks leading into the race. "In the Netherlands, it was not raced in your national federations. You looked around and you just saw all orange, and you realised all the helmets were also SD Worx, and it was very road rider dominated the last two years."That second year she came 26th, but it's hard not to think that 2026 promises far more. On Saturday Frain will once again line up in the front section of the field, after taking second overall in the UCI Gravel World Series this year, but many other elements have changed. For a start the race dynamics are expected to be wholly different his time. For a start, the shift for the first time outside Europe means there is no easy turnaround, and riders from other disciplines can't just drop in for a day, so there is less of a flood of European road professionals than in previous years. On top of that the nature of the course is completely different, heavy on climbing and gravel with more than 84% on the unpaved surfaces. This combination has made it a year where more and more key gravel specialists are turning up, raising the prospect that just maybe this year the road professional podium domination could come to an end. "I would love to see an actual gravel rider winning the rainbow jersey, just because I think for the sport, seeing that at races will be really valuable," said Frain. "But yeah, of course, the best rider will win."Just as the race situation has altered, so has Frain herself. Now into her second year as a full time gravel racer, having swapped over to Factor this year, and with an impressive list of wins right from claiming the Oceania Championships at RADL GRVL right at the start of the year to four UCI Gravel World Series race wins and also victory at the Unbound European qualifier of Heathland Gravel. She has proven that she is a force to be reckoned with on gravel, so hopes are high that Frain could just be a rider who can show off the green and gold colours of the nation's jersey near the front at its home World Championships."It's definitely been one of my main targets," said Frain. "I've been putting a lot of the effort around that and prioritising everything into this period, so then it's always a little bit more personal pressure, I guess, because you know you put in a bit more effort here, and so you want to see a good outcome that you feel proud of as well."There was some interruption to the preparation, with a bout of influenza stopping her in her tracks a couple of months ago, but having worked back from that it's now almost time to see what the results of that work and targeted focus will be."Generally it can suit me, if I'm having a good day," said Frain of the 125km course with 3,179m of elevation gain. "It does get more towards that heavy end of climbing for me, but then it's hard for everyone. So yeah, if I'm having a good day, and anybody that is smart about it can come away with a good result there, I think."Though, no matter what you do in preparation gravel remains unpredictable and sometimes that's a blessing and other times its a curse."It's still gravel, and anything can happen. Puncture risk is higher and things like that," said Frain. "So you just try not to put too much emphasis on the race because you just want to be happy with whatever you put in."But at the same time, yes, it's super important and it is a good opportunity for me to get a nice result and that would ,of course, be the dream."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Can cyclists actually avoid injuries and illness? Experts examined three years of UAE Team Emirates-XRG data to find out
item.author: James Witts
item.content:encoded: Less unusual is an unusual fact: “There are significantly more crashes on the right side than on the left. We can’t explain why. We’re looking into it.” The words of Raaghib Fredericks, UAE Team Emirates-XRG doctor, at this July’s Science & Cycling conference in Barcelona, where the South African presented his provisional findings on the injury and illness rates at the world’s leading cycling team for seasons 2019 to 2021. That crash bias was a footnote to a fascinating hour that revealed why staying injury- and illness-free is the most significant (albeit unsexy) performance boost a team and its riders can enjoy… “What do we currently know about injuries and illness at WorldTour level?” asks Fredericks. “Very little. There have been nominal studies in this area, including terrific research entitled ‘ by a team led by Dr Thomas Fallon [of Queen’s University Belfast]. We set out to add to Fallon’s work.”Fredericks’ research covered 30 male cyclists and analysed injury and illness data from the team’s cloud-based medical database, which was updated weekly. He could then compare those rates against training data from TrainingPeaks, the idea being that by pinning down injury and illness rates against factors like training loads, UAE Team Emirates-XRG could integrate protocols and best practice in search of, if not preventing and eliminating, at least ameliorating the impact of injuries and illness, which are significant. “Over the three seasons analysed, we lost 1,920 racing and training days to illness and injury,” he says. “That equates to around two lost days per rider each month.”That absence varied from one day to months, as in the case of Diego Ulissi, who the team announced in mid-December 2020 would stop training and racing immediately after an irregular heartbeat led to a myocarditis diagnosis. The Italian was given the green light to resume training the following February, before racing again at mid-April’s GP Miguel Indurain. The 37-year-old now races for XDS Astana after making the switch for the 2025 season.From a team’s perspective, a broken rider is like a broken wheel: useless. His or her impact is felt by the team, with schedules changed and, depending on the rider, chances of victory diminished. The competitive impact is felt commercially, framed against cycling’s fragile business model. Losing your strongest riders equals fewer wins equals less media exposure equals a struggle to attract sponsors… It’s a domino effect of doom. Injury has a real and quantifiable impact on a rider’s transfer or contract value, too. The European Sport Management Quarterly, Journal of Sports Economics and Applied Economics have all featured research that shows injury can impact market valuation by 10 to 20%, with that rising to over 30% for a serious or recurrent injury. It’s worse news for older riders, as this can approach 50% for those on the wrong side of 28 years old. Naturally, this drop in market value limits an athlete’s salary and earning potential. Egan Bernal is a clear example. In 2019, the Colombian won the Tour de France at the age of 22. In January 2022, he signed a lucrative five-year extension with Ineos reportedly worth €2.5 million to €3.0 million annually. Later that month, he suffered over 20 broken bones, a punctured lung and chest trauma after hitting a parked bus at 62km/hr. Since then, though he’s shown glimpses of his past form, he’s not been the same rider. His contract with Netcompany Ineos runs out at the end of this year and, at the time of writing, though there are rumours of either another extension or a move to Movistar, his future remains unclear. What is clear is that his likely next deal will see a salary drop to €2 million or less. Still healthy, but a sizeable percentage drop.Time off the bike has clear consequences, so the aims are prevention (the ideal) and limitation (the reality). In Fredericks’ analysis, those 1,920 lost days were broken down into 140 incidences of injury and 134 incidences of illness.When it comes to injury, 68% occurred during racing (compared to 32% in training). That’s significant and even more so when you account for annual workload. While training volume nestles between 18,000 and 23,000km, racing is around 8,500km. All in all, a rider is four times more likely to crash during a race than training.No one was seriously injured, and all riders started the next day. “That was a positive,” says Fredericks. “But I’m just glad I wasn’t the doctor at that race. He had to dress and undress the injured six riders for up to 12 days, adding an extra two-and-a-half hours to his day. Injury has significant implications for the staff as well as the riders.” (The doctor clearly did a fine job. This was the Grand Tour where Pogačar introduced himself to the world, finishing third and winning three stages in the process.)Jayco AlUla doctor Luca Pollastre agrees that traumatic injuries are the most common. “While the frequency of crashes is relatively stable, the severity of those crashes is rising, which can mean weeks or even months before an athlete can return to competition,” he says. “We feel this is due to the aggressive nature of racing.”The most common trauma in Fredericks’ analysis was what he euphemistically termed ‘superficial’, like the road rash Pogačar endured at La Vuelta. Then came damage to bones – fractures or breaks – which shines a spotlight on bone health, a hot topic in professional cycling. Fredericks revealed that a significant number of riders [over 50%] had low bone mineral density, and quite a few of them are actually osteoporotic. Treatment includes bone-strengthening medication, calcium and vitamin D supplementation, and weight-bearing exercise. “But that raises an important quandary,” says Fredericks. “We want to protect the riders from the risk of a fracture, but will they be interested in running, which we know helps? And will they be happier for more weights if it adds weight? It’s tricky.”Damage to muscles, tendons and cartilage followed, while in Fallon’s research, hand and head injuries, particularly fractures and concussions, were common, with head injuries the most prevalent for female riders.Overuse injuries are far less common, says Fredericks, with the majority related to patellar tendinopathy and Achilles tendinopathy, which are the result of the repetitive load of thousands of pedal strokes outpacing the tendons’ ability to recover and adapt.Arguably, their rarity is credit to bike-fitters, like Phil Cavell, co-founder of Cyclefit in London, who have worked with many professional riders, including the Lidl-Trek team. Cavell’s also an author, whose most recent book, The Cycling Addiction, has just come out.“To be fair, bike-fitters are only one reference point WorldTour riders are triangulating off,” says Cavell. “There’s also advice from teams and, surprise, surprise, WorldTour trends. Sometimes riders make decisions not wholly based on bike-fit and physio-led opinion.”Cavell says there are hotspots when working with WorldTour riders, most notably when myriad factors change, like the bike, shoes, saddle and pedals, which can happen if a team’s sponsors change or a rider moves. “That’s when team camps become dawn to dusk affairs,” he says. “There may be adaptations at the foot, knee, hip, back… These adaptations may express over time, so our job is to predict what’s going to happen and put in place mediations.”“I remember working with a very good rider, recently retired, who started a particular Grand Tour with a 17cm drop from saddle to bars,” he adds. “It worked okay for eight or nine days until it didn’t. We were brought in to revise his drop with a bit more insight and data – saddle pressure-mapping, motion-capture. He could see his issues reflected in our findings.”Fredericks’ research also focused on the impact of illness, explicitly seen in February 2020 when the UAE Tour was abandoned with two stages remaining due to an outbreak of Covid-19 at the UAE Team Emirates’ hotel in Abu Dhabi. The Emirati team and three other squads were quarantined for two weeks while health authorities carried out tests. Soon after, the team’s lead sprinter, Fernando Gaviria, confirmed that he had contracted coronavirus.Of the 134 incidences of illness between 2019 and 2021, Fredericks says that 41% of these occurred during racing, with the remaining 59% either in training or between races. “In that time, we had 11 recorded cases of COVID, resulting in a loss of 137 race days [out of 659 lost to illness as a whole]. That’s significant and came down to the minimum 14-day isolation period, plus a graduated return to racing.”Obviously other teams suffered. Take Simon Yates at Jayco AlUla, who tested positive after stage seven of the 2020 Giro d’Italia, held in October, and withdrew. The Australian outfit’s staff members also tested positive at both the Giro and late August’s Tour de France. The pandemic’s impact is still felt by Jayco, albeit positively.“We have systems in place that stem from that experience,” says Pollastre. “These range from the use of face masks to strategic room allocation for athletes and the careful assignment of therapists to individual riders, among many other measures.”“At the beginning of each season, we strongly recommend influenza vaccination for both staff and athletes,” he continues. “During the season, the team doctors hold a weekly call to review the health status of all riders. Relevant information is then shared with coaches and sports directors to support performance-related decisions. Understanding wearable technology data, training loads and providing continuous education are key components in minimising risk.”Still, despite best practice, it’s hard to avoid SAD (Seasonal Afflicted Danger). “We always expect more issues at the start of the season due to the weather and changes in environment, moving from Australia to the Middle East and then into the European season,” adds Pollastre. “Towards the end of the year, there can also be a spike in illness due to the cumulative fatigue of the season. Although we haven’t analysed it over seasons, at our team I believe that a loss of approximately 10% of training and racing days per rider per year is a realistic average.”Pollastre says that upper respiratory infections are the biggest cause of time off the bike, which matches both the data from Fallon and Fredericks’ research: “Of the 134 incidence of illness, 60 were respiratory related, like upper respiratory tract infections.” That’s around 45%. Fallon’s study found that racing Grand Tours is associated with a spike, potentially due to “immunosuppression” through the three-week strain. Load management is one method to reduce the chances of falling ill, but that’s clearly more controllable in training than at a race.Dermatological issues, like saddle sores, were responsible for 18% of lost days, with gastrointestinal issues close behind – ideally not too close behind – at 17%. Interestingly, in Fallon’s research, female athletes report a higher ‘burden’ of gastrointestinal symptoms than the males, although the reasons are not fully understood. suggested that this disparity could be down to hormonal changes affecting gut motility and sensitivity.Looking ahead, Fredericks is planning to pore over more recent data in search of solutions. What those solutions are is highlighted by Fallon’s research, which ranges from the use of protective clothing, such as Dyneema-enhanced jerseys to help reduce the number of abrasion-type injuries to neck-strengthening exercises, particularly for female riders, to minimise linear and rotational acceleration of the head during a crash. “Cycling should also embrace technological advances in the use of head-impact accelerometers that feedback to the race doctor’s car to improve care and assessment,” the paper reads. The problem is that the root causes of injuries and illnesses are multifactorial and somewhat speculative, albeit speculation stemming from education. Cavell gives the example of those traumatic injuries. “Does the trend of a more forward centre-of-mass with narrower bars mean less reaction time if something does happen? And what about shorter cranks? They allow a rider to maintain a deeper drop without blocking the hip, but does this have an effect?” As for the right-side crashing bias mentioned earlier, “That almost certainly has to be correlation, not causation, unless a parcours is especially right-corner-focused.” Ultimately, for all the sophistication of modern professional cycling, staying healthy may still be its simplest performance advantage. Crashes remain an unavoidable hazard, while illness and overuse quietly erode seasons too. Fredericks’ research shows how much time is lost, but also where gains might come from: better data, smarter load management and preventative care. The marginal gain could be staying upright.

item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘We will remain solely focused on preparing for the start of the season’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: The Knicks lost their second consecutive official scrimmage on Thursday……only for the organization to announce on Friday morning that nope, they ain’t budging and entering contract-extension negotiations any time soon.Gotta love how the outside world sees this as the excrement hitting the fan while we are here resting easy still enjoying the championship.On the plans for extension-eligible Karl-Anthony Towns, Josh Hart, and Deuce McBride:“As an organization, our entire focus is on preparing for the upcoming season and delivering another year for our fans to be proud of. As a result, we will not be negotiating contract extensions until later in the season and will remain solely focused on preparing for the start of the season.”On the Knicks’ announcement:On why the Knicks needed additional time away from basketball after winning the championship:“If you think about it, we played a long time last year, and our summer was short. So the guys needed to get away from the game. They needed to go fill their cup, however that may be.“And so our demands weren’t the same as other teams. Going around the league and talking to other teams since they’ve come back, some of them have been working since July and August in terms of training camps here and overseas camps and in [Los Angeles] and Miami and voluntary camps and back in the home gym.“We encouraged our guys to get back at the end of September, but it wasn’t mandatory. We didn’t really push hard for our vets to come back. I told them to fill, whatever they wanted to do, and take some time and when you’re ready to come back, come back.”On his straightforward approach to free agency:“It was pretty chill, honestly. I knew I wanted to come back here, so it was easy.”On not considering offers outside of New York’s“We really didn’t listen to anything else. I told my agent and everybody that I wanted to come back here, and if the money situation worked out, I wanted to come back. Not do anything else.”On embracing a different role with the Knicks this season:“I know it’s not my regular role that I’ve played before I got here. But it’s something I’ve fallen in love with, and I love playing my role and playing for this team and playing for each other. I think that was the biggest thing last year that I’ve learned.”On prioritizing winning over individual statistics:“For us, it’s not about numbers. It’s all about winning the game and doing anything to win the game. And I think a lot of us put things behind us to make that common goal happen.“And that’s from the coaching staff to everybody down the line. I think we all got to understand on what it means to be a part of this team and a part of the Knicks. So I think that’s been set, and that’s why I wanted to come back. I love the standard. I love the culture here.”On seeing the Knicks’ three championships represented on their jerseys:“I just liked seeing the number three at the back of the jersey, the championship number three.”On Bruce Brown’s potential contributions to the Knicks:“I’ve known Bruce for a while. Everything I’ve seen from afar as a competitive I’ve seen in these couple weeks here. I think the things that he can do for us can be very helpful”On his impression of the Knicks from afar:“They’re super tight. Great locker room. Goofy, fun crowd to be with and be around. It shows why they won last year”On how the NBA’s second apron impacts all kind of players:“I’m sure there is. The new CBA is good for max guys, new free agents and rookie extension guys. The middle guys, it kind of sucks for us. There’s not a lot of people getting that full mid-level”On playing at Madison Square Garden as a Knick:“It’s kind of surreal. Grew up a Knicks fan and the fact that I’m sitting in this locker room. I’ve always wondered what this locker room looks like”On the Clippers’ curse and asking the franchise to change its name:“I do think the Clippers are cursed. I told [Steve] Ballmer to change the name when he first got here and everyone kind of laughed at me.“They definitely need to change the name. This…energy is still on this franchise.”On attempting to fight D’Angelo Russell after the leaked video scandal:“I tried to get to the arena, they had security and everything. They stopped me at the door, told me I couldn’t come in, take a couple of days off.”“I had the whole gang with me. It was about to go crazy.”On his reaction to D’Lo leaking the video:“I ain’t never been in a situation like that where my teammate just snitched on me. I was like, ‘they’re gonna call me a punk in the media,’ and I’m mad for real, I gotta do something. I gotta show him. I know he’s young, 19, 18 or whatever, but still you don’t do nothing like that.”On arranging retaliation against Russell’s brother:“I still had to get him, so while he was playing, a couple friends of mine had to get his brother in the family lounge and all that. I had to get some type of get-back.”On why the alleged retaliation never became public:“It’s the Lakers. There’s a lot of things that go on in LA. LA is no place for the weak.”On the false report that LeBron James confronted him for arriving late to practice:“Yeah, it sucks, but what can you do? It’s unfortunate. I don’t know. One, I’m sure we can check. I don’t know where that came from. It never happened. And two, at the end of the day, I don’t know — I think we just got to focus on ourselves. There’s going to be a lot of outside noise to pull us apart from what we’re supposed to be and what we’re supposed to accomplish. So, it’s important that we stay together and we keep our eyes down.”On feeling unfairly targeted by the report:“Yeah, I mean, I don’t know. One, the question I had was, ‘Why me?’ Those type of things I can’t understand. One, it’s not true. But then again, it’s like, ‘Why me?’ But then again, I guess I’m Joel Embiid. I’ve been in that situation. I don’t usually talk when it comes to those (rumors). So, it feels like I’m an easy target. But yeah, as long as we know who we are. And we just got to stick together.”

item.title: Lotto-Intermarché youngster announces retirement from racing after just two years in the peloton
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Lotto-Intermarché youngster Robin Orins has announced his retirement from racing after just two seasons in the professional peloton.The 24-year-old Belgian turned pro with Lotto-Intermarché last season but missed a large chunk of the year after suffering mental health problems, including panic attacks.He raced from July to October and took on 27 race days between March and June this season. He announced on Instagram on Thursday that he's decided to retire from racing."I’m stepping away from professional cycling," he wrote."It’s time to turn a page, filled with emotions, memories and lessons, both positive and negative. A page that shaped me into who I’m today, and one that will be talked about for years to come. It ends earlier than expected, but without regrets."Orins had excelled as an under-23 rider, claiming second place at the 2024 Liège-Bastogne-Liège U23 as well as two third places at Paris-Roubaix Espoirs, and top-five finishes in the under-23 time trial at the 2024 European and World Championships.However, Orins struggled upon joining the pro ranks, not making his Lotto-Intermarché debut until the Tour de Wallonie last June."The lights just went out. I felt mentally and physically empty. Everything made me tired," Orins said last summer. "I became afraid - of everything, but mostly of myself. I didn’t even have the energy to ride my bike anymore. I lost the joy of cycling."Last season, he raced Wallonie, the Tour of Britain, and Il Lombardia, among other races. This year, he made his season debut at the GP de Denain and rode several WorldTour races, including Itzulia Basque Country, La Flèche Wallonne, and Liège-Bastogne-Liège.His most recent outing, and it turns out his final race as a professional, came at the Belgian National Championships in June, where he took part in both the time trial and road race."After months of rebuilding myself, I got back on my feet. But I realised how much energy it had taken and how difficult it was to find the old Robin again. No matter how badly I wanted it, the downs were too frequent," Orins wrote."This year, I wanted to return happy instead of unhappy. I wanted to enjoy the bike, the people around me, the suffering and, above all, feel fulfilled again. But things didn’t turn out as hoped. No matter how hard I worked, my body said 'no'. Now my head and heart are saying 'no' too."Orins said his retirement is "like a breath of fresh air", adding that he wants to discover life beyond cycling, which he's done since he was six years old. He did, however, say that his retirement from cycling isn't the end of his sporting ambitions."Honestly, this feels like a breath of fresh air. There is more to life than cycling, and I want to discover that with my girlfriend, friends, parents and family."Cycling will always have a place in my heart. Every scar, trophy, tear and smile has its story. This is not the end of my sporting ambitions. As my friends say: 'A fox never loses its tricks.'"Thank you to all the people I love. Cheers! Voske OUT."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Netcompany Ineos add climbers Markel Beloki and Harold Tejada as Sam Welsford exits after just one season
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Netcompany Ineos have announced the arrival of two climbing talents, with Markel Beloki and Harold Tejada both joining the team for 2027, signalling a strengthening of the team’s climbing talent in a bid to return to the team's stage race glories of old.At the same time, the team will lose sprinter Sam Welsford, who is heading for his home squad Jayco-AlUla on a two-year deal.Rumours of both Beloki’s and Tejada’s arrival have been long-heralded, though the length of their contracts is unknown, with the British team using the phrase "from 2027" in their press releases.Both will provide much-needed assistance in the mountains as Netcompany Ineos hope to return to the kind of form that saw them win 12 Grand Tours with five riders across 10 seasons, though they have failed to hit the top step in a single three-week race since Egan Bernal’s Giro d’Italia victory in 2021.Only 21, Beloki is a strong climber with a huge engine, which brought him second place at the 2024 Spanish National Championships at the age of 18. His two professional wins are also indicators of his potential, with his GC success at this year’s Tour de l’Ain coming off the back of a solo move on a mountain stage in the three-day race. However, Beloki is yet to show his talents in Grand Tours. His results so far are nothing to write home about, as he failed to finish this year’s Vuelta a España, though a steady 35th overall in the Giro is decent for one so young. “My ambition is to develop as a stage racer and, in time, compete for results in the Grand Tours," Beloki said."I know that it takes patience and consistent work, so being able to learn from experienced teammates, contribute to their success and make the most of my own opportunities is something that really motivates me."At 29, Tejada is already proven, and while he’s not a regular winner, indeed he has just two pro victories; his most recent success came earlier in 2026 when he won a mountainous sixth stage of Paris-Nice. “Harold is a strong, solid climber with plenty of experience. He’s been consistently up there over the last few years, and he’ll be a great support to our GC riders," said the team’s cirector of racing, Geraint Thomas.Heading out of Netcompany Ineos’s roster, which currently stands at only 16 confirmed riders for 2027, is Sam Welsford, the Australian sprinter who has spent just one season at the team. 30-year-old Welsford is heading for Jayco-AlUla, where he’s signed for two years.Clearly talented, his season at Netcompany has not been as rewarding as both he and the team would have hoped, despite starting the season with a stage win at the Tour Down Under. Since then, he’s struggled for results, finishing in the top 10 on only six occasions, arguably not enough for a sprinter.His departure might also indicate Netcompany’s increased focus on stage racing, where they’ve historically been so successful, and also be a side effect of Dorian Godon’s success in punchy sprints. As Netcompany Ineos have chased Beloki, Jayco have been after Welsford for some time. "It is really great that we have been able to finalise this deal and have him on our roster for the next two seasons," said the team’s head of performance, Gene Bates."Sam is well known to the team staff and riders. We are really looking forward to working with Sam and his abilities on the road. He is really focussing on road racing now and in the sprints. He will add a great deal of motivation to the group, and having him allows us to focus on some big projects for 2027 and 2028."Welsford has ridden for a number of WorldTour teams since joining DSM in 2022, but sees this move as a homecoming."After five years racing at the highest level, it feels like the right time to come home and be part of an Australian team with such a strong history in the sport," he said."I’m looking forward to bringing my experience, continuing to develop and, most importantly, racing for something that feels very close to home. I’m really motivated to see what we can achieve together and proud to represent Australia on the world stage."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: A rare return to unpredictability as no Tadej Pogačar at Il Lombardia opens the door to the same anarchy as Worlds – Analysis
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: In the 25 Monument Classics since Tadej Pogačar won his first of cycling's oldest, most prestigious and hardest one-day races at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2023, 19 of the victories have been shared only by him and Mathieu van der Poel, with just seven different winners.The five other champions in that period are far from complete shocks: Remco Evenepoel twice, Wout van Aert, Matej Mohorič, Jasper Philipsen, and Dylan van Baarle.All more than 230km in length and offering up some of the most attritional routes seen on the cycling calendar, the Monuments have long been where the preeminent riders rise to the top, but even the era immediately preceding the arrival of Pogačar pointed to more of a democracy than the almost total duopoly we've been watching for the past four seasons. In the 25 Monument Classics before Pogačar sprinted to that maiden title in Liège, there were 22 different winners across Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix, Liège, and Il Lombardia, with only Jakob Fuglsang, Vincenzo Nibali, and Phillipe Gilbert as repeat champions in that time frame, and considerably more riders in play for the wins.As 2026 nears the final of the five, Il Lombardia, on Saturday, the racing should briefly be returned to the less predictable and – if the World Championships men's road race was anything to go by – almost completely lawless racing largely unseen since the Slovenian has established a vice grip on the majority of major races. Just as San Remo was for Eddy Merckx, Roubaix was for Roger De Vlaeminck, and Lombardy was for Fausto Coppi, Pogačar has made one of the five his particular playground of choice, and that has been the northern Italian race, matching the latter's record of five victories as he completely destroyed the field 12 months ago to maintain his perfect record.And anything but the sixth arriving this Autumn, and Italy's greatest rider being overtaken 72 years after he set what seemed like an unbreakable record, would've been one of the shocks of the season, no matter who was on the start list.But even Pogačar – despite his miraculous ability to avoid major injuries for the large majority of his career – is not invincible, and the most important crash in terms of impact all season, which left him concussed and with a fractured collarbone and vertebrae at the Vuelta a España, has changed the complexion of what likely would've otherwise been another tension-less Il Lombardia.Throughout his reign of five wins, the Slovenian has only grown more dominant as the years went on, too, winning his first two titles from two-up sprints against Fausto Masnada and Enric Mas – who showed the world exactly how to step into the void left by Pogačar as he soared to the Vuelta a España GC title last month, Spain's first for 12 years.But the unchanged variable of his perfect record has been UAE controlling the race on the approach to whatever the key climb is on the route, and preventing any of the previous chaos, randomness, and masterclasses at the eleventh hour of the season which long punctuated Lombardias gone by into the 2020s – shown best by the list of former winners – from developing. In truth, Pogačar is so superior that UAE haven't needed to rely on overly nuanced tactics whether heading to Bergamo or Como, instead just setting a brutal tempo before launching him into the final 30-50km, and to three solo wins at the last three editions – winning by 0:52 in 2023, a massive 3:16 in 2024, and 1:48 last season. The runner-up in those latter two was Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who seems the obvious successor on paper. However, as everyone saw at Worlds in Montreal, where that same theory was tested, the Belgian star is significantly less of a guarantee than his contemporary. What became clear in Canada is that the gap between Pogačar and the rest is much greater than that of the rest to each other, with Evenepoel likely starting on a par with UAE's leaders Isaac del Toro and World Champion Brandon McNulty, Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5), Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek), and Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike).Evenepoel going solo seemed likely before he was brought back down to earth in Canada, and while he can try to just follow the moves and somewhat rely on his sprint, the millimetres and controversial photo finish that saw him snatch the European title from Ciccone's grasp leave cause for nerves to creep in. Pogačar's brute force approach is what benefitted the Belgian most, particularly last year, with the earlier and earlier opening up of races ruling out anyone from even attempting to beat the UAE rider tactically.But thinking he can match that as the instigator could prove fatal for Evenepoel and Red Bull's chances, as it's easy to forget what the reigning champion has normalised when it comes to solo attacking, often matching records set by Merckx and Coppi with his daring, but now expected moves. With that should come what was true of Worlds: a war of attrition being matched by a total tactical battle, where the numbers game may prove as vital as it did for McNulty and the USA en route to rainbows. Evenepoel's greatest asset may end up not being his ability to solo or sprint, but whether Primož Roglič or Giulio Pellizzari can make it into the leading split to add more strings to his attacking bow, and the same can be said of UAE, who are probably still starting with the strongest team. McNulty and the US showed everyone the blueprint for how to win a Pogačar-less race at Worlds, and it was actually his compatriot Quinn Simmons who came closest to upsetting the usual flow of Lombardy a year ago when he made an all-out assault on the course from the early breakaway. UAE and Pogačar hoovered him up eventually, of course, and he faded to fourth by the time the race reached the finish, but knowing that the bullet from behind won't be anywhere near as threatening compared to the inevitability of the Slovenian, it could cause the early break to return as a genuine method to victory. Don't be surprised to see the stars and stripes of Simmons and several others all on the move to try and get ahead of Evenepoel, Del Toro and Seixas, as anticipation becomes genuinely threatening again. However, this would be returning cycling to an even older era if someone were able to pull it off, and the difficulty of the route cannot be sniffed at with 4,845m of elevation gain packed into the 243km.Mollema in 2019 provides the blueprintIt feels like a lifetime ago that George Bennett was battling away with the Astana duo of Fuglsang and Aleksandr Vlasov until the last 6km of the COVID-19-rescheduled 2020 edition in August of that year, or since Bauke Mollema's well-timed move in the last 20km of the 2019 race saw him emerge victorious ahead of a group of closely matched climbing stars like Roglič, Egan Bernal, and Alejandro Valverde. What was then an attainable goal for many, Il Lombardia became unwinnable in the years that followed for 99% of the peloton, and the same can largely be said of the other four Monuments. But with the door now open in Pogačar's absence, perhaps the biggest surprise win since Mohorić in San Remo in 2022 is around the corner – and even then San Remo has long stood as the most unpredictable of the five, so that run of predictable winners likely stretches back even further. Despite their importance in the context of cycling's history and Pogačar's place as an all-time great, the past three editions could have been an email in reality, with everyone, including his rivals, without wanting to admit it, knowing who was going to win barring major incidents.With the Slovenian returning to action in 2027, it may be the only chance some riders get to win a Monument for the next six years [when his newly-signed contract ends], so they must grasp it with both hands.Few outcomes would be as compelling as Evenepoel emerging victorious, though, six years on from the horror crash off a bridge which left him seriously injured and leaving the race in an ambulance. But it's hard to see anything but an incredibly complex race play out for the Belgian, so he will have to thrive amid the adversity as he did at the Euros and several races before. If he does succeed, the outpouring of emotion should be cathartic. Mollema will start Saturday's race as the oldest rider at 39, before his retirement, and it's his method to victory which looks most likely: all the big names together in the last 30km, before someone makes the right opportunistic move, and perhaps that could come from Evenepoel, or Seixas, the youngest man on the start line. This Saturday's race and a return to a more open Il Lombardia won't be one to miss. item.title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
item.author: Adam Morton in Nadi, Fiji
item.content:encoded: ‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in FijiWealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.Continue reading...

item.title: Thieves make off with €5m haul from prestigious Italian winery
item.author: Angela Giuffrida in Rome
item.content:encoded: Gang breaks into cellar of Marchesi Antinori in Cortona and loads two trucks with 30,000 bottles before getawayThousands of bottles of wine worth €5m (£4.2m) have been stolen from a prestigious winery in Tuscany in what is thought to be the biggest heist of its kind in Italy.A gang of at least seven masked individuals broke into the cellar of Marchesi Antinori, a family-owned winery dating back to the late 1300s, in Cortona after shutting off the alarms and surveillance cameras before using company forklifts to load two large trucks with 30,000 bottles of wine and making off.Continue reading...

item.title: Is Antonelli favoured by Mercedes? Wolff responds to latest claims
'I'm here to just go all-out and race without any regret' – Florian Vermeersch prepared for Gravel Worlds title defence
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Belgian racer Florian Vermeersch is in Australia this weekend, the 27-year-old taking aim to become the first rider to defend the gravel world title since the event was established in 2022.Now he's in Nannup, Western Australia, for another shot at the UCI Gravel World Championships, where he'll face off against the likes of Keegan Swenson (USA), Mads Würtz Schmidt (Denmark), and Matt Beers (South Africa), among others.Vermeersch has mostly focussed on the road this season, racing the spring Classics (including podiums at Omloop Het Nieuwsblad and the E3 Saxo Classic plus a top-10 finish at the Tour of Flanders) and the Giro d'Italia. But he's still prepared to defend his title at the Gravel Worlds, "Unfortunately, I've done only one gravel race. The plan was to do one or two more, but due to my calendar, it was not possible," Vermeersch told this week."But I've done a lot of gravel rides at home wearing the jersey, so I've enjoyed that. It was a very nice year, I would say. It's an honour to wear those rainbow colours."Vermeersch and his UAE Team Emirates-XRG team have planned for him to return to the gravel this week to keep the rainbow stripes in the team along with Brandon McNulty's road world title."From December last year, when we were speaking about my calendar with my team, I already got the signal that I could defend my title. They gave me the freedom that if I wanted, I could come here," he said."I said immediately that I would like to defend it. So it was a bit of a no-brainer. I didn't really have to fight for it with the team; they allowed me to come, so that's very nice of them and I really appreciate that."The last few weeks, to prepare and train for this race, have been very nice. I've made a lot of hours on the bike, and I think I'm in a good place."The 144km elite men's race route will include 3,713 metres of climbing and much tougher gravel than previous editions in Belgium, Italy, and the Netherlands, with at least 80% gravel on every route, said race director Stephen Gallagher."I did the big loop – the 77km loop – yesterday, and it's really tough. I think it's going to be a very demanding race, but I'm in for a challenge, and we'll see," Vermeersch said of the route."Some corners were actually pretty sketchy. It's really slippery, and you have to pay attention. But I think now, with the rain coming down, it's going to make it a bit faster and a little bit less slippery in the corners, I think. So for this, the rain is not too bad."He acknowledged that the route is a major challenge but noted that some pressure is off his shoulders, having already won the world title last time out."I think it's going to be on the limit. I'm a big guy, and it's almost 4,000 metres of climbing. But I'm in for a challenge. I really like the course, and we'll see where I end up."The good thing is I've already won the jersey once, so this is not an extra stress factor for me. I'm here to just go all-out and race without any regret, I would say. Just leave it all out there."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: The fastest road helmet we've ever tested has dropped by up to 40% – Save watts and money at the same time with this Sigma Sports deal
item.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
item.content:encoded: When it comes to the best aero helmets, there are plenty to choose from, but the fastest we've ever tested is the Oakley Velo Mach.In our in-depth wind tunnel testing of 47 helmets, the Oakley was the absolute fastest aero road helmet, saving up to 8 watts at 40km/h. It was only beaten by a few dedicated TT helmets, making it a serious contender for cyclists who want speed, safety, and cutting-edge design.It takes it down to just £169, from the usual £280, and a massive £111 saving. In our Oakley Velo Mach review, expert tester Tom Wieckowski scored it an impressive 4.5 out of 5. Along with that aero performance, he reckoned it was also stylish, comfortable, well ventilated, and ticked all the boxes for a top-tier road helmet.These Oakley deals are showing as limited sizing at Sigma, but there are three colour options to choose from, and the deal is for the MIPS-equipped version.It's worth noting that in testing, Tom chose a small over his usual medium, which is something to consider if you're pulling the trigger.It's also cheaper at , but the sizing is even more limited; if they have a size for you, it's an even better price.The Oakley Velo Mach is the fastest road helmet we've ever tested, and one of the most expensive. This discount takes it down to an incredible price, and if you want to find out why we rated this so highly, then now is the time. It's limited sizing, so you'll have to be quick. Cheaper at Alpine Trek, but not many options to choose from there.In his review, Tom summed up the Oakley by saying;"There's not much to dislike, really, and it hasn't given me a second of discomfort or any other issues in months of regular use. If you are shopping for a new performance road helmet, the Velo Mach should at the very least be one of the models you consider."Highlights for Tom included its ventilation, and with just three front vents, one large main one, and two side vents, which also double as sunglasses storage, it received a big tick there. Tom noted that the large front vent did the job of keeping things nice and cool despite the aero design.It was also very comfortable; of course, everyone's head is different, but having no hair (sorry Tom!), he added that he's more sensitive to uncomfortable helmet interiors than most. The Oakley delivered a great overall fit with zero issues over numerous hours of testing.Its aero performance is the real appeal of the Velo Mach, and it has two very cool rubber fins which protrude from either side of the helmet in the back quarter. These 'flow conditioners' are designed to reduce drag and increase airflow attachment, helping the air passing over the helmet's outer shell to stick to it for longer. It’s a feature that doesn’t appear on many helmets, and it certainly seemed to aid the aero performance in our wind tunnel testing.

item.title: Rocket Report: A rare Falcon 9 scrub; is it just about Vulcan's time to shine?
item.author: Eric Berger
item.content:encoded: Welcome to Edition 9.14 of the Rocket Report! The big news this week, from our perspective, is that United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket appears to be close to launching. We've seen a no-earlier-than launch date for the return to flight mission of October 29 (an Amazon Leo flight), and the next rocket up after that, also an Amazon Leo mission, is also planned for this year. Assuming the solid rocket boosters work, Vulcan could be poised for a major breakthrough next year in cadence.As always, we welcome reader submissions, and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.Nuri rocket notches another success. South Korea successfully deployed five satellites for its first domestically launched microsatellite constellation during the fifth flight of its homegrown Nuri rocket Wednesday, Yonhap News Agency reports. In addition to the primary payload of five New-space Earth Observation Satellite Constellation for National Safety microsatellites, nine of the rocket's 10 CubeSat secondary payloads were released as planned, according to the Korea AeroSpace Administration. PERSAT-02, developed by South Korean startup Quaternion, failed to separate from the rocket.

item.title: "It should be banned" - F1 drivers still divided over cooling vests
Lidl-Trek announce early departure of Giulio Ciccone on eve of final race together at Il Lombardia
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Giulio Ciccone will depart Lidl-Trek at the end of the 2026 season, having reached a mutual agreement with the German WorldTour team to part ways before the expiration of his contract, which was due to run until 2029. It means the Italian will ride his final race for them this Saturday at Il Lombardia, where he will lead the team alongside Quinn Simmons and Juan Ayuso, ending his time after joining from Bardiani in 2019 and managing 10 victories."After eight seasons together, the Team and Giulio have reached the mutual decision to part ways, which means Il Lombardia will be the Italian’s final race in Lidl-Trek colours," read a short statement released by the team on Friday."We want to thank Giulio for all he has done for the team and wish him all the best for the future."Ciccone won two stages of the Giro d'Italia, the Clasicá San Sebastián, and five WorldTour races in total with Trek, and wore both the yellow jersey at the Tour de France and the pink jersey at the Giro as race leader during his eight seasons. Lidl-Trek has undergone major changes this past season, with Italian General Manager Luca Guercilena departing after 16 years of leadership back in June. Andy Schleck has since taken over as CEO, with Grischa Niermann joining as Chief Sporting Officer.With Ciccone on the way out, Lidl-Trek's climbing core will be made up of Ayuso, Derek Gee-West, Mattias Skjelmose, and new signing Felix Gall in 2027. It also opens up a spot for more new arrivals, with Filippo Ganna being linked with a move away from Netcompany Ineos to Lidl-Trek in recent days by Ciro Scognamiglio at and Daniel Benson's Substack.If Pinarello Q36.5 is confirmed as his new team, Ciccone would instantly become a main leader alongside Pidcock, who could combine as a deadly duo in the hilly Classics, and as stage hunters or GC options in the Grand Tours.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Volkswagen's replacement for the ID.4 crossover is here
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: Volkswagen’s ID.4 is no more. The midsize crossover debuted in 2021, one of VW's first new electric vehicles designed in the wake of dieselgate. A year later, the company began local production in Chattanooga, Tennessee, and a couple of years ago facelifted the model, adding a much-improved rear drive unit in the process. But Chattanooga turned its attention away from the ID.4 earlier this year. And, having sold almost a million ID.4s (and near-identical ID.5s) globally, the German automaker has decided it’s time for its replacement. Meet the ID. Tiguan.Dropping the numerical and adopting the moniker of VW’s big seller is a statement. “The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars. The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together,” said Thomas Schäfer, CEO of the VW brand.VW was an early pioneer of using flexible vehicle architectures to create a multitude of bodystyles and sizes with common parts, and its transition into building EVs hasn’t changed that. The ID. Tiguan uses an updated version of the company’s mass-market EV platform, now called MEB+, with either 58 kWh or 77 kWh battery packs. The smaller pack is only available with a 187 hp (140 kW) rear electric motor, but the 77 kWh battery can be had with either a 281 hp (210 kW) rear-wheel drive powertrain or as a 295 hp (220 kW) all-wheel drive version. Range is up to 373 miles (600 km), at least according to the European WLTP test.

item.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
item.author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
item.content:encoded: Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river floodingIsaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.Continue reading...

item.title: ITA confirms 12-month ban for Kyrylo Tsarenko after three whereabouts failures
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The International Testing Agency (ITA) have announced that Ukrainian racer Kyrylo Tsarenko has accepted a 12-month suspension from racing after committing an anti-doping rule violation.Tsarenko was suspended from racing after three instances of late submission of whereabouts filings within a 12-month period.His period of ineligibility runs from July 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026, and he already resumed racing for Solution Tech-Nippo-Rali back in July. He has since raced the Sibiu Tour, several .2 races in Turkey, and a host of races in Italy, including the Coppa Sabatini, Giro d'Abruzzo, Tre Valli Varesine, and Gran Piemonte."The ITA reports that cyclist Kyrylo Tsarenko has agreed to the consequences for his ADRV under Article 2.4 of the UCI Anti-Doping Rules (UCI ADR)," the ITA announced on Thursday."Following three instances of late submission of whereabouts filings, which resulted in three filing failures within a 12-month period, the ITA and Kyrylo Tsarenko have reached an agreement on consequences in relation to the ADRV."The Rider did not challenge the ADRV and agreed with the consequences proposed by the ITA on behalf of the UCI, namely a one-year period of ineligibility and disqualification of results. Accordingly, the case was resolved via an agreement on consequences."Tsarenko continued racing to end the 2025 season, taking in 19 race days including the Czech Tour, several Italian one-day races, and the UEC European Championships road race.However, all of those results have now been wiped out as a result of the year-long suspension, while he was held out of racing for the first half of the 2026 season before returning at the Sibiu Tour, where he finished sixth."Considering that the rider was serving a provisional suspension, which he accepted on a voluntary basis pending the proceedings, the rider’s period of ineligibility ended on 30 June 2026. All the rider’s competitive results obtained from 1 July 2025 until 3 December 2025 are disqualified, including forfeiture of medals, points and prizes," the ITA announced."No party with a right of appeal has challenged the decision before the Appeals Division of the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The case is therefore final."The ITA will not comment further on this case."

item.title: 'They are going to be hard to beat for sure' – Marianne Vos toes the line against a field packed with discipline specialists at the UCI Gravel World Championships
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: When Nannup was first announced as a venue for the UCI Gravel World Championships, one rider who immediately looked forward to the 2026 rainbow jersey race in Western Australia was Marianne Vos. It wasn't close to home, far from it, and it wasn't the perfect parcours, but it was definitely somewhere she wanted to be.While Vos wouldn't go so far as to call herself familiar with the area, she does have history, after coming out for the Margaret River Tour, which swept through the region multiple times around a decade ago. The organising team for that race then shifted focus to SEVEN and, almost as soon as the UCI got into gravel, put up their hands to host a series race and were in the queue for a World Championships."I already knew that SEVEN was the event they were doing every year, but being held in May it was always difficult to get here in the road season," Vos told as the event neared. "But as I did also do Gravel Worlds over the last two years, when it fitted my road schedule and when it fitted the team schedule, I was very keen to also do it now.""When it first got announced, I was already excited back then." "First, yes, I wanted to go here because it's here," said Vos of the Nannup location for the world title battle. "Next to that, just to get here and try and get to the best level I can, especially after a difficult season. I know winning will be difficult and really hard, but trying my best and getting the best out of the race – that is the goal and the focus."Vos already knows what it is to win a Gravel World Championships, just one of four elite women in that category, as she claimed the rainbow stripes in 2024 and she also came second to compatriot Lorena Wiebes in 2025."If you look at the altitude metres of the race, there's no doubt that it's hard and there's also no doubt that the climbs, although they are not long, add up all the time. In the end it will be a challenge," said Vos."I think in gravel it's a combination of physique, a bit of tactics, a bit of technique, and that combination is what I like most about gravel. And, in the end, on this course for sure, the best riders will end up in front. I guess besides mechanicals or crashes, normally the best rider will win, so that's a good thing. It will be a fair and honest race."Riders like 2024 Unbound winner Rosa Klöser, who won at Sea Otter Europe in the middle of last month, where Vos was third, and this year's Unbound winner Sofia Gomez Villafañe, who has barely been off the top step this year, are among the field heavy in gravel specialists who have been drawn to an event which is expected to open the door for them.It would, of course, be ridiculous to question Vos' off-road prowess – she has, after all, won eight cyclo-cross world titles to go along with the gravel rainbow jersey – but it's not been her day in and day out in recent times."All the disciplines get more and more specialists, so does gravel, and there are some roadies, some mountain bike riders, so it's still a combination of the different disciplines. But for sure, the gravel riders, they are experienced in gravel riding. So in this kind of racing, when it adds up, when you have to constantly be alert on the course, it will be tough competition," said Vos."I mean they do this all year and they are going to be hard to beat for sure.""I think it's an honest course, so in the end, the better riders will end up in front, so tactics can play a role for sure and as a Dutch team, you want to help each other as much as possible," said Vos. "You for sure don't want to be in each other's way. But on this kind of course, I guess in the end it's also about individual qualities. So there is this combination of riding for the country and trying to get the best out of yourself on the day."'If it was easy then it wouldn't be fun'Whatever that is, after the race celebrations or commiserations, the prolific world title winner will be taking some time off to reset as she looks forward to a more settled year ahead."I'm looking forward to next season, yes for sure," said Vos. "To rest first and to have a proper build-up again ... just getting back to the normal routine and trying to get the best out of yourself."No matter what that best looks like, in an evolving women's cycling environment where it's getting tougher and tougher to cross the line first."It is, but of course, as a team you try and make a plan to get the best result possible, and that's what you work towards. Actually, all these changes in women's cycling and the growth, and also it getting more and more professional, also means you need to adapt and focus and refocus, and in the end just get 100% out of yourself to be competitive," said Vos. "That's maybe the main reason to still also have this extra motivation and spark to go for it because it's never the same and there's so many new races and the competition is tough, and teams have changed."Vos is now 39, and it is two decades since she won her first elite world titles, but the rider with a lifetime contract at Visma-Lease a Bike's genuine enthusiasm for the sport is showing no signs of waning."It's a constant challenge, which keeps it also very exciting and, yeah, it's not easy to win, but if it was easy then it wouldn't be fun. So when things work out – even though sometimes it might take a while, or even though there's also difficulties – that's still pretty exciting. The racing itself is beautiful, and also the training is something I like. I think it's a combination of things that keeps me excited and motivated, and I still have fun."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.content:encoded: Cyclingnews subscribers get early access to all of our new bike review videos before they go live on YouTube. To join our ever-growing community of cycling-obsessed subscribers and support our world-class cycling journalism, join Cyclingnews Endurance bikes have for so long been the slightly plodding, dull siblings to their racier counterparts, or cooler all-road siblings. Canyon seems to be trying its best to redress this with the new Canyon Endurace, the top spec model that has been raced at WorldTour level, but how does it fare for the likes of you and me?Our Tech Writer, Tom Wieckowski, has been putting the bike through its paces on his home roads, testing it with race wheels, and adds in his experiences of the old model, the Aeroad it competes with, and the Cannondale Synapse too. As one of the perks of being a subscriber, you can watch the full video review now before it goes up on YouTube in a couple of weeks. Not a subscriber yet? item.title: Tour of Chongming Island: Lorena Wiebes storms to 21st victory of the season on stage 1
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: The Dutch rider easily moved away from Clara Copponi (Lidl-Trek) and Lara Gillespie (UAE L'IMAD) in the final run to the line at Chongming New City Park on Friday, claiming her 21st victory of the season. By the time the race reaches its conclusion on Sunday, it's likely Wiebes will have upped that tally to 24, with two more stage wins and the general classification title looking the most likely outcome over flat terrain.Wiebes has managed the hat-trick of stages before at the Chinese Women's WorldTour event, back in 2019 when she was racing for Parkhotel Valkenburg, where she also won the GC, points, and best young rider's classifications.SD Worx weren't forced into doing all of the work on the laps around the southern part of the island in Shanghai, but did have to react to a late move from Ruby Roseman-Gannon (Liv AlUla Jayco) in the last 6km.Everything was brought back before the final 2km, with Lidl-Trek, Jayco, and UAE all taking up the position at the front of the peloton at times, but Wiebes was always lurking with Barbara Guarischi ready to do the final lead-out. Gillespie had managed to get herself in between Wiebes and her final lead-out rider, but she was jumped by the Dutch rider, who kicked out of her wheel for another dominant victory, the 139th of her already incredible career.Wiebes is expected to win again on Saturday's stage from Changxing Island Country Park to Chongming New City Park, with another flat 129.4km route on offer.Lorena Wiebes
