item.title: Canyon Endurace CF SLX review: One of the fastest and most capable endurance bikes on the market right now
item.author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
item.content:encoded: $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999 8.24kg out of the box, incl. storage accessories, tubes and integrated computer mount. (no pedals)DT Swiss ERC 1600 Dicut (35mm) Crystal white / Champagne (pictured) / Atlantic blue The update and launch of the Canyon Endurace generated a lot of chat in the run-up to Paris-Roubaix.Canyon split the launch of its latest endurance road bike, launching the top-tier Endurace CFR, which was designed to help Mathieu Van der Poel win Roubaix first, and then announcing the second- and lower-tiered CF SLX, CF, and Allroad models a little later on.The latest Endurace CFR really looks like an Aeroad, the brand's aero race bike, and has almost identical geometry numbers. The Endurace CF SLX that you see here has less racy geometry. In fact, Canyon calls it 'an aero bike with all-day fit'. Canyon sent me the Endurace CF SLX 8 in 'Champagne' colourway to test; it's one click down from the top-level CF SLX 9 and comes in at $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999 for the Shimano Ultegra, carbon wheel-equipped model. The Endurace has a slightly cheaper entry price point than the Aeroad, and is a lot less than the top-spec Endurace CFR, but there's not much in it. When do you buy the Endurace, not the Aeroad? The Endurace has been considered one of the best endurance bikes for a while now, and the bike's latest update saw it get faster and more aero with bigger tyre clearances and slightly more stable geometry. I've ridden this bike on the road exclusively for several months, and have even stripped it back to race a local hill climb. This bike is at least a must-consider if you are shopping for an endurance bike around this price point. My size small bike came in at 8.24kg out of the box with a storage bag and accessories, computer mount, TPU tubes and no pedals. Unless you order the bike with a storage bag and accessories, which aren't included as standard, you can expect it to be a couple of hundred grams lighter than this. It depends on what you might order and fit to the bike, but it's around this mark. Canyon has changed a fair bit on the Endurace this time around; frame design, geometry and componentry have all changed. When it comes to the frame, the biggest visual change comes from the altered seat tube and chainstay junction shape. The seat stays are also more aero, and the bike has a new seatpost. The round S15 VCLS 2.0 flex seatpost has gone, as has the 'Comfort kink' seat tube cutout. The CF SLX now has a comfort aero post in the form of the SP093 VCLS Aero seatpost, which the brand says increases compliance by over 25% compared to a rigid equivalent. CF models will still come with the round VCLS post, which for me offers more comfort. Fun fact: you can swap in the rigid Canyon equivalent, which is of course what the Alpecin pros like Jasper Philipsen did when they rode the Endurace CFR. The frame has received aero tweaks and has been to the wind tunnel. The headtube is aero bike-narrow when viewed from the front, and it's clear that aerodynamic performance has been a consideration even on this second-tier model. Canyon tested this bike in the GST wind tunnel in Germany with a lower leg dummy across a 20-degree yaw angle sweep, with bottles and cages, 65mm DT Swiss wheels with a 29mm Continental Aero 111 tyre up front and a 30mm GP5000 S TR tyre in the rear. Average system drag at 45km/h for the Aeroad CFR, Endurace CFR, and CF SLX models was as follows: So, according to Canyon, there are about 5 watts in it. If you're shopping for an endurance bike and are told it's only about 5 watts slower than what a WorldTour pro is riding, I think that's positive news at face value. This bike also isn't as stiff, which stands to reason. I asked Canyon for some stiffness numbers too for context, and it sent me over some info, in Newton-meters per degree for the head tube (HT), and Newton-metres per milimetre for the bottom bracket (BB); a bigger number in each case being stiffer:HT: 98,1 Nm/°HT: 114,5 Nm/°HT: 103 Nm/°From Canyon's numbers, we can get some context here on what to expect from the CF SLX; it's slightly less stiff in the bottom bracket and softer at the headtube. I've ridden and raced on an Aeroad CFR, and whilst you can feel the difference, it isn't a gaping chasm. I'll talk about this more, because with this endurance bike getting racier, I want to highlight what you can expect from the CF SLX's riding performance if you are considering one. What else is new for the CF SLX? Well, the top tube storage hatch has now gone; it's been moved to the down tube. The bits in the tool roll could rattle against the top tube on the old bike; things are silent now, and there's more room. It's a good change. Tyre clearance has also been boosted to 38mm from 35, providing room for even bigger rubber. My bike came stock with Schwalbe Pro One Evo 32 mm tyres. Starting with 32mm tyres does boost comfort. The CF SLX can also be fitted with Canyon's Endurace CF SLX Fast Fender set, which comes in at £119.99. The fenders quickly fit to semi-permanent mounts which are fitted to the bike frame. You can of course just fit a clip-on guard, but they tend to need more fiddling with. It's a valuable option if you are considering this model as a winter bike or all-round workhorse, though clearance will be reduced to 35mm with them. The Canyon Load tool pack costs £19.99 and doesn't come with the bike, so you will need to buy a frame storage bag at the least to take advantage of the built-in storage space.I'd also recommend just mentally adding £33.99 / $39.95 to the cost of the bike you may be looking at, as you will need to buy the Gear Groove computer mount, which neatly integrates with the handlebars. There isn't really another option apart from O-rings and a basic mount. Canyon doesn't tend to include mounts or many accesories. It would be nice to see the proprietary mount included with the bike, or just the price increased to cover the mount and eliminate a bolt-on at checkout; it feels a bit clunky to me, especially now that many brands include specific mounts. The CF SLX 8 comes with a dependable Shimano Ultegra Di2 groupset with a 34-50 chainset and 11-34 cassette. You also get a 4iiii P3+ left-hand crank-based power meter; I found its numbers a tad jumpy compared to some dual-sided PM pedals, but it's nice to get one included for the price. Endurace bikes now come with shorter cranks; depending on size, bikes have 160, 165 or 170mm cranks, to facilitate more comfortable positions and opening up riders' hip angles. My size small bike came with 165mm cranks. There's also the integrated CP0048 PACE T-Bar with new 'compact' drops. The Endurace stock handlebar is 390mm to 440mm wide, with three adjustable settings via a pair of T25 Torx bolts under the bar tops. The bars have a 108mm drop and an 8-degree flare. If you want a narrower handlebar, you will need the Race Drops with their 350 and 400 mm width, but they are going to set you back £219.99. It would be really nice to see these as an alternate option when speccing the bike at checkout. The CF SLX also gets the Canyon Sport Geometry; the CFR has different Sport Pro geo. Compared to the previous Endurace CF SLX, the chainstays are 3 mm longer, the wheelbase is 16mm longer, and the effective stack and reach are pretty much identical. The last Endurace CFR I rode was a real hot hatch; this updated model does feel a fraction longer to me, and just a little bit calmer in the handling department. I've ridden a size small and am 176cm in height; my bike came with 165mm cranks as mentioned, an 80mm stem as standard, and has a stack and reach of 565mm and 386mm. Whilst that 80mm stem size may seem too small, I've ridden endurance bikes with longer stems that felt shorter; the Canyon geometry is well designed to make life easy, whilst still keeping everything looking good. I think if you're a rider that needs a longer reach, double-check things, but this being an endurance bike, you're possibly on board for shorter reach numbers anyway. To compare that to the recently launched Trek Domane in a Medium (an equivalent size for me) that I rode, the CF SLX is 10mm taller with a 12mm longer reach. Compared to a size small Aeroad, the Endurace is 26mm taller and 4mm shorter. My previous best-ever recorded power for one minute was set riding the Aeroad CFR a couple of years back; I improved on that number in my final week of testing on the Endurace. Of course that doesn't mean this bike's faster than an Aeroad, but I share that information to show that it's a competitive bike with racy performance. This isn't a boring, endurance machine that can't be ridden hard. 'More speed, Captain' has been my train of thought for harder rides on the Endurace; I personally want a narrower handlebar. Coming from the 35cm Hyper bar I rode on the Winspace M6 left me disappointed at first and has been one of the things that makes the bike feel less quick for me, but I've adapted to the wider bar over time. I've swapped in the new Dura-Ace C50 wheels I'm testing at times with fast 28mm tyres to sharpen things up, and they do extract more speed from the bike; a quicker pair of wheels does add more speed to the Endurace. Switching back to a 32mm tyre and lower pressures does introduce more comfort and just calms things down, which is great for everyday riding. If this sounds a bit like you, the Aeroad or even the Endurace CFR (though it's expensive) is probably going to be the model to go for. If you purchase this bike and then constantly look for ways to make it faster, it's probably the wrong choice. Though the prospect of a fully aero, race-spec Endurace with that higher front end is an intriguing one. But if that is the case, the Aeroad or Ultimate, depending on what you need, are the way to go. However, Canyon has, in my opinion, brought its endurance bikes even closer to its race ones with this update; the differences are finer in many areas. This is a key point to convey: the Endurace is a fast, capable bike with racy characteristics; it's just more comfortable and versatile. The ride experience from the Endurace has been very good. The handling for me is just a touch calmer and slower than the previous bike, probably due to that longer wheelbase. Handling and cornering on the bike are excellent; no concerns there for me. Diving into corners or braking hard are tackled with ease. Canyon has created a very capable overall handling package. The geometry is also very balanced; it's an impressive blend. The bike doesn't feel too short or sit up and beg, but I can still achieve my usual hunkered down on the hoods aero position. However, due to that shorter reach and taller stack, I'm locked into the hoods very comfortably. I can also ride the bike slammed with ease due to that taller front end, and the saddle-to-bar drop makes it look attractive. It's not as stiff and zippy as an Aeroad, or another full-blown race bike, and that's part of the feeling I miss slightly. It's not electric to ride, but the experience is still very pleasant. I can't say I feel much ride smoothing from the new VCLS aero post; that's not to say it's not doing its thing, though. I think tyre and pressure will do the heavy lifting for you when it comes to smoothing things out. With a 32mm tyre, or bigger, the ride is refined and smooth.The shallower DT Swiss wheels are also a good call for me; their 35mm rims just make things that little more user-friendly and aid the handling compared to a deeper, more aero wheelset. It's a nippy yet comfortable wheelset and pairs very nicely with the good-quality 32mm Schwalbe Pro One tyres. The stock Fizik Aliante R5 isn't a saddle I'm crazy about; the way its profile changes shape, rising near the nose, makes it hard for me to get truly comfortable. I'd probably change it, but as ever with saddles, it will come down to personal preference. The only niggle I've had from the bike came from the saddle rail adjustment bolt, which worked loose, meaning the saddle dropped forward at very annoying times on a hard ride until I torqued it to spec. Saddle fore-aft and angle adjustment bolts are seperate, which makes life easy, but it's the second Canyon model I've experienced it on, so do check this bolt after a few rides, which you should be doing anyway. Everything else has been perfect on the bike, and I've had no issues. I feel riders are familiar with Canyon's adjustable stem and bar platform now, and it is very easy to adjust. Just look after it long-term to prevent any issues. Maintenance and servicing The key maintenance considerations when it comes to the Endurace CF SLX are front-end related. The integrated Canyon handlebar assembly will need to be looked after long-term to help minimise big workshop labour bills. A full strip-down for headset bearing replacement won't be that cheap.Minimise front-end blasting when washing, and consider a mudguard or the Canyon fender set for wet weather riding to look after those headset bearings. Check bolt torque specs every so often, particularly the pair of Torx bolts under each bar top, and the stem bolts. I'd recommend something like six-monthly-ish headset bearing cleaning and re-greasing just to stay on top of them and prevent them getting into a real state; that's when things will get expensive. The CF SLX comes in at $4,200 / $4,499 / $5,999 as pictured, a very competitive price for the solid spec, which includes a power meter. Don't forget the £80 / $99 Canyon shipping and packaging fee at checkout. For me, you get more value with this spec than a range of other big-name endurance bike competitors that I have tested personally. Don't forget there's also the 105 Di2-equipped bike for slightly less cash, the performance will be on a par with Ultegra overall. It's a good chunk of cash cheaper than a similarly specced Specialized Roubaix endurance bike, and if you want an equivalent Ultegra Di2-equipped Domane from Trek, you will spend over $1,000 more. Ditto the Cannondale Synapse, which, for a similar Ultegra Di2 spec, costs £6000 / $6,499.The Ridley Grifn RS endurance bike is another competitor with similar performance, which I rate, but the CF SLX also has it beaten on price by a fair chunk of cash. The Endurace spec is solid, with no gaping holes or weak points; yes, you might want to change the saddle, and you will need to buy at least the Canyon computer mount. Canyon's direct-to-consumer pricing has a lot of its big-name competition beaten on price and in performance.The Endurace CF SLX is an excellent all-round endurance bike that sits at the faster, performance-oriented end of the endurance bike spectrum. It isn't as stiff or as exciting to ride as a full-blown race bike, but it isn't too far off at all and offers a competitive, comfortable, and confident riding experience that will welcome you pushing it hard and going fast or tackling an all-day adventure. The taller front end and more relaxed geometry are still purposeful, but it's more user-friendly than the Aeroad or Endurace CFR geometry. If this is a key concern for you, and you don't need a massive amount of reach, don't chance the Aeroad and regret being too stretched out or low; go for the Endurace.Throw in the 38mm tyre clearance, which gives you plenty of room for bigger comfort-boosting tyres, improved down tube storage and the ability to run full fenders, and you have one of the most well-rounded endurance bikes out there right now.After months of exclusive riding on the road, I'm in agreement with Canyon's statement that this is 'an aero bike with all-day fit'. An improved design that boosts aero, clearance and frame storage. A nice looking frame and fork and block colour options. The frame tube shape changes update the bikes looks too. Very solid, with no real gaps. Ultegra di2 is great, DT Swiss carbon wheels and 32mm Schwalbe tyres and the Canyon finishing kit is all solid. I'm not totally sold on the saddle. Very good. Not race bike exciting, but this bike can do everything well. Will respond if you are riding hard, but the geo makes it very comfortable. Sure footed handling that's a touch calmer than the pevious model. 8.24kg out of the box with accs. Might just dip inside 8kg without accesories. Not that light, but doesn't create any ride feel issues and there's scope to drop weight. Very good, a very competitive spec for less money than a lot of competitor endurance bikes on the market with the performance to go with it. There is also a wide range of cheaper models.

item.title: Line on course for move up table in Autosport National Rankings
Will Carlos Baleba fix Manchester United? Three big questions ahead of potential debut
item.author: Graham Ruthven
item.content:encoded: As the Premier League returns, we dive into the signing who could boost United’s midfield – or confuse things furtherCarlos Baleba cost Manchester United $88.7m (£65m) plus $6.8m (£5m) in add-ons when they signed him from Brighton in August. He may be worth even more now despite the fact that the Cameroonian has yet to debut for his new club. Many United fans are counting on Baleba to be a one-man solution to their early-season problems. No pressure.An ankle injury kept Baleba on the sidelines as Michael Carrick’s side struggled against Everton, Manchester City and Fulham. The 22-year-old joined United just a few days after the opening-weekend defeat to Hull City, so he’d already had a preview of his new team’s troubles to come. item.title: British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents | Gordon Brown
item.author: Gordon Brown
item.content:encoded: We have a deep reservoir of assets, but struggle to turn small companies into global success stories. Innovation needs to be at the heart of government policyGordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010The coming 10 years are almost certain to be the decade that sees the greatest scientific breakthroughs in a century. The question is whether advances now under way in AI, quantum computing and biology can address cancer, find ways to treat or prevent dementia, and overcome the growing resistance to antibiotics. Can we find sustainable ways to address our energy needs and protect the environment at the same time? Can AI transform the way we deliver education, health and social care to the benefit of millions, as well as advance modern manufacturing strength? And what role can Britain’s inventors, investors and industrialists play in developing these transformative technologies?While the US and China are the world’s obvious innovation powerhouses, the UK also has enormous assets, as the Innovation Nation Conference in Manchester addressed by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will hear today. We are home to four of the world’s top 10 universities and 16 of the top 100, five of which are in Europe’s top 10 for spin-outs, startups based on intellectual property produced through a university’s research. With less than 1% of the world’s population, the UK produces 6% of the world’s research papers, nearly 9% of citations and 12% of the most highly cited research.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010Continue reading...

item.title: Three course features that could be make or break at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: The course for the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup, Western Australia, is carved out of a landscape that delivers so many options for a gravel race and the SEVEN UCI Gravel World Series event has, over the years, tried and tested a number of them. The outcome as the organisers now deliver the rainbow jersey race is an unrelenting 144km course for the elite men and a 125.6km route for the elite women.It will be a test with 3,179 metres of vertical gain for the women and 3,713 metres for the men on what are described as 'Liège–Bastogne–Liège climbs' as the course winds its way through the course in the Blackwood Valley. 'Draining' seems to be the word riders keep using when asked how the course is after they've had a chance to ride it for the first time. It's the type of route where it's hard to say there are any easy portions, given there is at least 84% gravel, often long undulating plateau sections once a climb is completed and then descents where riders need to keep their wits about them so they don't slip out on the pea gravel corners. Plus it's unrelenting right to the finish.There are, however some patches which stand out, from sections that could split the field early or create the opportunity for a final winning move, so now it's time to take a closer look at those.Brockman – First shots firedThis isn't the first climb of the race, that honour goes to Killarney at just over 15km in, but at just 1km long with a 7.6% average the history of SEVEN has shown that it's the climb coming at around 27km into the day of racing that will start to make the difference. It's usually where the first major selection is made."You are going to see if you've either got good legs or bad legs on Brockman," said race director Stephen Gallagher.The 2.4km Brockman ascent has an average gradient of 8.2% and what's more the terrain that comes after is enough for riders to dig in and try to hold on to any advantage that they reap. There is a descent off the top, but not a long one, and then the profile just plots a jagged course for the next 20km, pulling in the climbs of Adina. The real stretch of descending only comes at over the 50km mark, before a flattish section of around 10km that offers some repreive before the climbing begins all over again.Ellis Creek – The fatigue finderThe climbs continue, and so does the wear and tear which is perhaps why Ellis Creek's 2km, 9.1% average with 169 vertical metres gain hits so hard. The challenging climb that also delivers an extra bit of steepness near the top – comes just after 85k of racing for the men and at around 65km for the women. Plus there is no real relief once you make it over the top."I think you've just got fatigue in the legs by that point, so that's why it's the hardest and I think it's deep enough into the race where you can go from there to the finish line," said Tasman Nankervis, the 2023 winner of the elite men's race at SEVEN who also raced this year at the UCI Gravel World Series event which replicated much of the World Championship route. "The year I won it, I broke away from there," he said referring to the Ellis climb. "It's logical to make a move from there, whereas to make a move from Brockman, that's a bit of a high risk manoeuvre. It can be done, but you can win the race from Ellis, so I think people tend to go more in from there."The Folly climb is a new introduction for this year, part of the finishing loop which will take the riders close to the start line but then send them off for more, including the 2.4km effort with a 4.8% average gradient that is Folly. It's bound to be packed with spectators, as it is just a short walk from the start/finish line and comes at a point where there is just over 20m of racing remaining.It starts with riders turning on to a short but relatively steep bitumen section and then it's another turn onto the dirt, which, after a little recent rain is nicely packed down and while there are a few small rocks strewn around and some ruts in some patches they are easily avoidable as it is wide and the main line is smooth.There is a reprieve part way through the climb which opens up to views of the rolling farmland hills, but then it just kicks in again.Nankervis warns that this climb isn't one to be taken lightly, with a need to have something in reserve, recounting that in his race at SEVEN this year a puncture had left him behind but he made up around ten positions in this sector as it was one where the lights went out for many. "It's really hard," added race director Gallagher. "It gets quite steep at the top. You can potentially go solo from that point if you're really strong, or you can certainly reduce a group to one or two riders."Then before riders hit the line there are still a couple of nasty pinches and the more gradual Lindsay climb on one last descent before the winner of the rainbow jersey is decided.Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Mikayla Harvey and Oliver Bleddyn set to strengthen Jayco-AlUla women’s and men’s rosters for next two years
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: GreenEdge Cycling have announced two additions to their structure, with New Zealander Mikayla Harvey joining the Liv-AlUla-Jayco women’s set up and Australian track star Oliver Bleddyn arriving at the men’s Jayco-AlUla squad.Both riders have signed with the Australian WorldTour teams on two-year contracts, taking them to the end of 2028.While Bleddyn is best known as a track rider, where his successes include a gold medal in the Team Pursuit at the Paris Olympic Games, the 24-year-old has plenty of experience on the road. This year, he was second in the time trial at both the Australian and Oceania championships and joined the team as a stagiaire with Jayco-AlUla at the start of August. Since then he completed the Arctic Race of Norway, but has struggled since, finishing only one of seven late-season Italian Classics."I’m really excited about what next year can bring. There are some great opportunities ahead and I’m super keen to make the most of them," Belddyn said in a team press release. "The Tour Down Under would definitely be a special race for me to do. To race at home with this team is an opportunity I’d be really excited about."The team’s head of performance, Gene Bates, is looking forward to working with Bleddyn, saying, "he has got a huge engine"."He is a great and enthusiastic young rider and is also gaining a lot of experience on the road, riding as a stagiaire with the team this second half of the 2026 season. We are confident Oliver will be a great addition to the team in many different roles," Bates said. Harvey arrives after two years at SD Worx-Protime, and similar stints at UAE Team ADQ and Canyon-SRAM already behind the 28-year-old climber. Working mostly as a domestique, Harvey is able to take her leaders deep into hilly finals, and has the engine to bring breakaways back on flat days.Though she began this year with second place in both the time trial and road race at the New Zealand nationals, she didn’t start her European season until the Ardennes Classics in April. A crash took her out of the Giro d’Italia Women in June, since then she’s struggled to regain consistency, crashing out of the Classic Lorient Agglomération and the Faun Tour Femmes, where she suffered a concussion. "I am already looking forward to next season," Harvey said. "I am a rider that has experienced a lot, and I feel like I can add this to the team. Alongside this, I am a rider that is not afraid of trying something and being outside my comfort zone. I love attacking and dynamic racing. Especially looking for breakaways and escaping from the peloton."The team expect her to play a big role in hilly races, including the chance to race for herself. "Over the past few seasons, she has played an important support role, but with us she will also have the chance to race for her own ambitions again," said Head Sport Director Wim Stroetinga. "We strongly believe she has the talent and ability to be competing at the front of races and fighting for victories, and we are excited to help her take that next step."Neither men’s nor women’s programmes have been especially active in this summer’s transfer market, Bleddyn joining Will Holmes as the only two signings to the men’s squad so far. At the same time, not only are they about to lose Luka Mezgec and Luke Durbridge to retirement, and Mauro Schmid to Pinarello-Q36.5, a number of other riders are still to announce their futures with the team.On the women’s side, Harvey is the only new arrival revealed so far, though Erin Boothman has been promoted from the structure’s Continental development team. item.title: Six-day American Criterium Cup summer schedule confirmed for 2027 while USA CRITS taking shape for spring - North American Roundup
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: For a third year, the American Criterium Cup will include six stops across the central and western US to determine overall individual and team champions among well-established criterium events. Races will take place from June 11 to September 5, with Saint Francis Tulsa Tough establishing the first leaderboards in Oklahoma and the finale at the Bommarito Audi West County Gateway Cup in Missouri.The Tour of America's Dairyland will host the second race in Milwaukee, Wisconsin on June 26, with the third race, the Bailey & Glasser LLP Twilight Criterium in Boise, Idaho on July 10. After the August 1 Fulton Market race with Chicago GRIT, the series swings back to the west for the Salt Lake Criterium in Utah on August 7, and then a month later, the winners will be decided in St. Louis.The 2027 season marks the seventh for the ACC. Last year each event offered a $16,000 prize purse for pro women and pro men, with the series paying out an additional $44,000 to series winners across several classifications. Plans for any live streaming broadcasts have not been confirmed.Skylar Schneider dominated the women's competition this year, holding the red leader's jersey from start to finish, while Justin Williams made it a L39ION of Los Angeles sweep in the individual rankings taking the men's top spot. L39ION also won the team titles, the men's team title decided on a tiebreaker against Team Cadence Cyclery p/b Waldo Racing at the final event in St. Louis.Claudia Marcks (Pedla Racing Division) took the sprint classification across the six races by a single point over Holly Breck (L39ION of Los Angeles), while the men's green jersey as best sprinter went to Owen Gillott (Chaney Windows and Doors Big Shark p/b Pastaria).USA CRITS, the spring block of one-day races in the southeastern region of the US, will return for an 18th edition in 2027, anchored by the Athens Orthopedic Clinic Twilight in Georgia on Saturday, April 17. Races in Greenville, Spartanburg, Suwanee and Winston Salem were expected to return following Athens, with additional events still "being nailed down" to bring the series to eight total, according to Gene Dixon, founder of USA CRITS and owner of series producer Swagger LLC. The bulk of the calendar will focus on races across Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, the final calendar set in the coming weeks.Dixon said the emphasis was to provide a compact 30-day window to simplify travel for riders and teams, especially those traveling from outside the US. A similar prize purse to this year is expected, totalling $200,000 for individual races and overall series classifications with equal payouts among the men's and women's elite riders. All USA CRITS races will provide live streaming, produced by Swagger.Liza Ray (Kingdom Elite Racing) and Leonel Rodriguez (MC Cycling Team) won the individual titles in 2026.Next year's Amazon Armed Forces Cycling Classic, June 5-6, will introduce a UCI 1.2-level road race as part of two days of elite men's racing and continue with back-to-back criteriums for elite women. Organisers confirmed that the equal prize purse of more than $30,000 would remain in place.Last week reported that the UCI calendar had added two new men's races to the 2027 America Tour, Battenkill in New York on May 22 and the Amazon Armed Forces cycling Classic Capitol Cup in Washington, D.C. The long-running AFCC weekend will continue with a full schedule of USA Cycling-sanctioned criteriums, Capitol Cup on Saturday and Clarendon Cup on Sunday."This change reflects the vision we share with our partner Amaury Sport Organisation (A.S.O.) for the event's future," said Robert Laybourn, president of Arlington Sports, Inc, and the event race director. "Every major decision we make is guided by documented metrics and data. The event will continue to evolve and be refined as our budget and other constraints allow, pursuing changes that offer proven value to its growth, success and long-term sustainability."Organisers at Arlington Sports have not published a schedule yet, however, they have indicated to that the men's course will take place on a 20km (12.5-mile) circuit, the exact distance is yet to be determined. The race is expected follow directly after the early Saturday start of the Challenge Ride, where non-competitive riders have a three-hour window to complete up to five laps of the same circuit.Then the event will showcase the elite women as the final action of the day, held on the same 1.4km course as last year situated in front of the US Capitol building and the National Mall.Clarendon Cup events, now in a 29th year, will return to nearby Arlington, Virginia on Sunday. Last year omnium titles for the two days of racing were won by Marlies Mejías (Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY28/Deloitte) and Brody McDonald (Modern Adventure Pro Cycling).Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of both the UCI Road and Gravel World Championships, alongside the final monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Feds get ready to rewrite car headlight rules
item.author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
item.content:encoded: One of the regulations that make vehicles in the US different from those in Europe or Japan is our headlight rules. They’re laid out in the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), and changing them is—or used to be—a lengthy, laborious process, which is a major reason automotive lighting technology has lagged in the US. But the current administration says it’s time for “bolstering driver safety, slashing red tape, and embracing new technologies,” so it’s going to start a negotiated rulemaking process to rewrite the regulations to suit 2026.“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Jonathan Morrison said. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”

item.title: RIP Margaret Hamilton, whose code saved the Apollo 11 Moon landing
item.author: Jennifer Ouellette
item.content:encoded: Margaret Hamilton, who coined the term "software engineering" and led the development of onboard flight software for NASA's Apollo program in the 1960s, died last week at the age of 90. A recipient of the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Hamilton was also immortalized as a LEGO minifig the following year—part of the "Women of NASA" set that also included astronauts Mae Jemison and Sally Ride.“To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer—to say she was ahead of her time—would be a dramatic understatement. She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy, and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved,” said Olivier de Weck, interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics. “The Apollo program still stands as one of our greatest testaments to the power of collaboration, ingenuity, and engineering, and Hamilton was a fundamental contributor to that program’s success.”Born in 1936 in Paoli, Indiana, Hamilton graduated from Earlham College in 1958 with a degree in mathematics and a minor in philosophy—the latter a nod to her father (a poet) and grandfather (a headmaster). She married her first husband, James Cox Hamilton, that same year. The plan was for her to work until he finished his law degree, after which he would support her through graduate school to earn a PhD in mathematics.

item.title: Evenepoel and Del Toro the favourites, but Il Lombardia is wide open – Analysing the contenders
item.author: Patrick Fletcher
item.content:encoded: The final Monument of the 2026 season, Il Lombardia, is upon us and we have a fantastic race in prospect thanks to a fascinating array of contenders, who we're going to delve into right here.We've been adjusting to a Pogačar-less racing scene in recent weeks, and for all that it's a shame to have the world's biggest star on the sidelines, the racing has undeniably been more open, tactical, and interesting as a result.That's what we're expecting to see again on Saturday, at a 120th edition of the Race of the Falling Leaves that follows the Bergamo to Como direction on a 239km route with a finale over the Madonna del Ghisallo, San Fermo della Battaglia, and Civiglio climbs.We arguably have two top favourites – though neither so superior as Pogačar – and a rich array of names who will all feel they have a shot at a Monument on Saturday afternoon.After winning the European road race title, the Belgian has steadied the ship that listed so dramatically in the World Championship, and as such he starts as one of the top two favourites. As Worlds underlined, Evenepoel is a rider who can blow extremely hot and extremely cold. A one-pitch, know-what-you're-getting Pogačar he is not, but then again, that's part of what makes him such a compelling bike rider.In a Pogačar-less world, Evenepoel – a former world champion, two-time winner of Liège-Bastogne-Liège and five-time winner of the Clásica San Sebastián – ought to be the next man up. 12 months ago, he soloed to second place behind Pogačar rather convincingly, as he did repeatedly last autumn. But despite bouncing back from that off-day at Worlds, you sense Evenepoel is not quite at the height of his powers.The Europeans felt like a good example of a race he might have won solo at his peak. Indeed, he had to outsprint Giulio Ciccone for the second time in just a few weeks. Now, Evenepoel's sprint is an underrated weapon that only broadens the way in which he can win these big races, but you can't help but feel that the more we've been impressed by it, the more we've seen it in action, and the less that means he's actually been able to get away.Even so, he remains one of the very top favourites to finally win a race that he looked like he might have won as a 20-year-old in 2020.The rainbows may be wrapped around the torso of Brandon McNulty, and while the US rider will have more freedom than if Pogačar were present, it's Isaac del Toro who represents the best shot for UAE Team Emirates and a joint favourite alongside Evenepoel.Del Toro has all the tools to win this race. As the Tour de France runner-up, he has the climbing legs. As the winner of nearly every late-season Italian classic last year, he knows what he's doing in this punchy part of the world. And as the winner of the GP de Montréal in a sprint, he has the finishing speed to win if he has company.Del Toro has had a remarkable season in which he has won three WorldTour stage races, finished on the podium of his first Tour de France, and won a WorldTour one-dayer at Montreal. His performance at the World Championships in the same location was widely debated and shot through with allegations, and while we will take his ride at face value, there were tactical question marks that – like we saw at the Giro last year – could do with being ironed out.But on his day he is just the complete package, an electric racer, and he has a huge opportunity here to take the biggest win of his career so far.It would be rude not to give the world champion his own section. After all, Brandon McNulty's Worlds win, though highly tactical, was no stroke of fortune. He has largely operated as a domestique, but the immense talent that was evident so early in his career has never been far from the surface, and he had racked up a very respectable palmarès even before the world title.Since he pulled on that rainbow jersey, he has looked invigorated. Some of it might have something to do with Pogačar's recent absence, but he's been launching attacks left, right, and centre in a sign that the jersey is not weighing him down with any sort of onus of suddenly winning all the time now, but rather giving him a boost of confidence and a spring in his step.It will be interesting to see how he dovetails with Del Toro. The Mexican might be the standout favourite, but Pogačar is not back yet, and while that's the case there's room for McNulty to go after this race, and perhaps make a bit of a statement over his status in the pecking order at UAE.The Frenchman takes to Lombardia to round out one of the most extraordinary seasons we've seen in recent years, one in which he rose to the top echelon of the sport and became the most hyped man in professional cycling. Seixas looks likely to win this race in the future – you could say that about a lot of races – and while it wouldn't be a total shock to see him do it this year, excitement surrounding the recently-turned 20-year-old has dampened somewhat compared to his blistering Spring. Back then, he was genuinely looking like the second-best rider in the world with runner-up finishes behind Pogačar at Strade Bianche and Liège-Bastogne-Liège, either side of a complete evisceration of the Itzulia Basque Country field. He was fast-tracked into his Tour de France debut, and since then a touch off the gloss has worn off, with a more subdued racing style and a level just a notch lower. That's no slant on Seixas. Fourth on debut at the Tour de France at 19 is still otherworldly, and he only lost the GP de Montréal in a sprint against Isaac del Toro. But the World Championships, where he cramped in the finale, highlighted some - to be expected - limitations, and also the level of pressure he puts on his own shoulders, berating himself for riding like a schoolkid. However it lands, and he has all the tools to win it, Lombardia represents the final act of a breakthrough season and the start of a reset that may well lead to a different beast in 2027.Ciccone has shown his one-day shape is where it needs to be in recent weeks. As at the Europeans, he was out-sprinted only by Evenepoel at the end of the QP de Québec, and he was sixth at Worlds after looking momentarily like he might make his way across to McNulty alongside Tom Pidcock on the final lap.It's hard to see him winning in an outright sprint against some of the riders on this list, but as shown by the way he took the fight to Evenepoel at Europeans, he has the race craft to make different things happen. When he's in this form and this mood, Ciccone is fantastic to watch. And after the Europeans, he may even be riding with a little extra fire in his belly, which, for a rider who has always ridden on emotion, might just make an all-important difference.You never quite know what you're going to get with Tom Pidcock, which is probably why he's so exciting to watch. On his day, he's world-class, as evidenced by a palmarès that includes Strade Bianche, Amstel Gold Race, and a Grand Tour podium, along with all his off-road titles. His challenge to Pogačar at Milan-San Remo this Spring was another reminder of the levels he can reach on his day. But he can also look pretty ordinary, make mistakes, or fade away in big races. It can be hard to read his form, but it looks pretty good. He had a subdued Tour de France and then won the Mountain Bike Worlds, so it's been a tight one to adjust for a late-season full of hilly one-day races, but he seems to have done a decent job, winning on comeback at the GP Industria & Artigianato and featuring prominently in every race since, with podiums at Tre Valli Varesine and Giro dell'Emilia. He was also top 10 at the GPs de Québec and Montréal, and in the World Championships, where he was one of the very strongest in the group behind McNulty.He was also the most generous, and that's probably the most reliable thing about Pidcock – that he'll commit and go all-in for the win rather than playing games and riding for the podium. With no co-leader on his level at Pinarello Q36.5, it leaves him slightly exposed, and he may find himself in awkward situations on Saturday once again. But if he can take that small step towards his sparkling best, then he is well in with a shout of a first Monument title.Matteo Jorgenson has looked incredibly strong in recent weeks – just a vision of perfect posture and, in contrast to some of the more spritely climbers on this list, pure seated horsepower. The World Championships would indicate that Jorgenson would thrive in a more grinding, attritional affair, but he still had the punch to follow Tom Pidcock's decisive acceleration at Tre Valli Varesine. The big weakness in Jorgenson's arsenal is his sprint finish. He barely has one. So he'd need to win alone. And that's certainly not out of the question given the lack of Pogačar and given the potential room for tactical manoeuvre.In that respect, we need to highlight Visma's two-pronged approach, with Davide Piganzoli another credible candidate for the Lombardia title. More on the young Italian in a minute, but what's clear already from the past few races is how well they've combined. Piganzoli, of course, won the Giro dell'Emilia, and much like Brandon McNulty's world title, it was massively aided and abetted by Jorgenson's presence, strength, and actions in the group behind. The pair both attacked in the finale of Tre Valli Varesine, and this time it was Jorgenson who got to play the finale, but was third in the three-man sprint. Is Jorgenson just the perfect second fiddle, or can he become the main man in Como?We've mentioned some of Piganzoli's results, and his collaboration with Jorgenson, but the 24-year-old Italian deserves his own slot on this list. He has had a fantastic breakthrough season, shining as the top mountain domestique at the Giro d'Italia won by his teammate Jonas Vingegaard, and finishing eighth himself in the process. He was then drafted into the Tour de France squad late on, and in truth he was unable to reach his Giro form at any point during the race, but still ended up in 14th place overall. He went on to win the Tour of Luxembourg – his second stage race title of the season after the Route d'Occitanie – before his brilliantly-taken solo victory at the Giro dell'Emilia, which has propelled him up the list of contenders for Il Lombardia.Are we getting carried away here? I'm not so sure. The 20-year-old Belgian just won his first pro race, at Tre Valli Varesine, outsprinting two riders higher up this list in the process. With that, he has put himself at the forefront of our minds ahead of Il Lombardia.And yet, he is far from a reliable contender for this race. For starters, it's his first Monument, his first real test in a race as heavy as this in terms of distance and climbing. Secondly, the stunning talent that Widar showed in the U23 ranks has only come through in patches this season (which is absolutely fair enough). Thirdly, Widar is more of a puncheur than a climber, and while the climbs individually suit him, it's far from a given he'll stay the course here.That said, it was only recently that he was the best of the rest behind Pogačar on a big mountain stage of the Vuelta to Andorra. And when it comes to a sprint, he showed in mid-week that he has one of the best. He may have surprised Pidcock at Tre Valli, but the Briton responded quickly and got nowhere near him.It could go one of two ways, and while he might fall away completely, you wouldn't count him out of being in podium contention.Ben Healy hasn't hit the heights he did during his fantastic run of form in 2025, but there have been signs that he's getting back there after a difficult 2026 campaign. The Irishman was 8th at GP de Montreal, 10th at Worlds, sixth at Giro dell'Emilia, and in the main group at Tre Valli Varesine.He has been an attacking presence throughout. This is Ben Healy, after all, and that's not going to change. The question mark comes over how he uses those bullets. What we've seen in the past few years is a scattergun approach that has often rewarded him but elsewhere has seen him effectively set fire to whole mountains of energy. At Worlds, for example, he launched a big solo attack to reach the front of the race and by the time he'd done so the rest of the group were pretty much back there as well – a long time in the wind when he could have been in the same situation for a lot less money.But that's what people love about Ben Healy, and if you don't take those risks, you perhaps don't get the rewards. He is capable of a top result here, but needs things to go his way for that magic bullet to land – you can be sure he's going to fire the shots.Enric Mas did not finish Worlds and was 29th at Giro dell'Emilia, but we're not going to forget about his stunning Vuelta a España performance all that quickly. The Spaniard filled the void left by Pogačar's early exit and dominated the rest of the race with physical and tactical prowess. Mas has had a really bumpy few years, but when it's his day, it really clicks, and he can look like he's on the cusp of those riders in the very top bracket. Just cast your minds back to the 2022 Lombardia – he was the only rider who could get near Pogačar, and he put up a decent fight in the two-way sprint for the title.So while the past couple of races haven't been anything to write home about, Mas has performed here previously, his form can't have disappeared, and he has absolutely no pressure on his shoulders.The Italian isn't the biggest star, but he has been operating at a consistently high level for a couple of years now, and he comes into Lombardia with a list of results that reads: 2nd at GP Industria & Artigianato, 3rd at Giro della Toscana, 4th at Coppa Sabatini, 18th at Worlds, 3rd at Europeans, 7th at Tre Valli Varesine. And his one-day record hasn't been far off those levels all year; he has only won one – at Challenge Mallorca – so far (though he did win the Green Mountain stage and the overall at the Tour of Oman).He probably likes things a little punchier, so the long distance and the climbing load of Lombardia represent an even bigger hurdle to that top step of the podium. But then again, he was eighth and in the second group behind Pogačar at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in the spring.It's difficult to see Scaroni winning, but he's definitely an outsider for the podium.We focused on Evenepoel at the top of this piece, and he's definitely the focal point, but Red Bull's team is stacked with riders who might be leaders in other outfits: Florian Lipowitz, Jai Hindley, and Giulio Pellizzari.We went big on Ciccone earlier, but Lidl-Trek also have Juan Ayuso, who is becoming increasingly inconsistent but has the raw talent to win this race, while Quinn Simmons may find it too climbing-intensive but is sure to show off the Stars and Stripes with an attacking display.While we're on the subject of strong teams, none are in standout form but are here with Antonio Tiberi, Lenny Martinez, Santiago Buitrago, Pello Bilbao, and Jakob Omrzel. was a protagonist at Worlds, was third at Giro dell'Emilia, and looks like Netcompany-Ineos best bet here. also have the small matter of a former Olympic champion in Richard Carapaz.Tobias Haaland Johannessen leads Uno-X alongside the impressive Anton Charmig.We've mentioned Widar but is perhaps Lotto-Intermarché's more tried-and-tested top-10 contender.In Mathys Rondel, Marc Hirschi, and Michael Storer, have a decent set of potential top-10s.

item.title: Egan Bernal says his 'intention is to start the upcoming season' but admits question marks over his future
item.author: Owen Rogers
item.content:encoded: Egan Bernal has stated his intention "to start the upcoming season", but the winner of the 2019 Tour de France has admitted there are question marks surrounding his future.Bernal posted a personal statement on his social media on Thursday, after the journalist Daniel Benson reported on his Substack that he was weighing up his future, including the possibility of retiring at the end of this year. Bernal, who confirmed he had ended his 2026 season after the Tour de France, indicated that he will race on into 2027, but his statement was hardly categorical. "First of all, I am under contract with the team until the end of 2029, and right now, my intention is to start the upcoming season," Bernal wrote, confirming that his season.Further down his statement, he added: "I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now."The 29-year-old has been with Netcompany-Ineos since 2018, winning the Tour the following year and the Giro d’Italia in 2021. He has also taken victories at Paris-Nice, the Tour de Suisse and others. However, a training crash in January 2022, while training at home in Colombia, left him with career-threatening injuries, including a punctured lung, a broken rib and a broken leg, and he was away from racing for eight months. Since returning in August 2022 he has only won four times, three of those in the Colombian national championships. And while he occasionally shows flashes of his old brilliance, he is unable to compete with the current crop of GC stars."After so many years dedicated to cycling, I feel I have given the best years of my life to the sport - both as a cyclist and as a person," Bernal wrote. "I have made sacrifices I never imagined, won races that once seemed like impossible dreams, and experienced both incredible highs and very difficult lows; yet today I can look back with peace of mind, proud of everything I have done and achieved, with no regrets. "Over time, I have also learned that this sport isn’t just about results, victories, or sacrifices. It is also about enjoying the journey and finding the motivation to keep doing what you love."This year, I decided to end my season after the Tour de France. I felt I needed some time for myself - to rest, disconnect a little and regain the sense of calm that can sometimes be lost amidst the relentless pace of competition."I have spoken with the team and the people around me, and we are alone the same page: I want to give myself the time and space needed to face what lies ahead with the same conviction and dedication I have always had."I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now. For now, I want to enjoy the present, experience this moment calmly, and let time take its course."Subscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘At the end of the day, everybody has a short-term memory’
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: New York will watch the Knicks play basketball inside the Garden for the first time since they waved them goodbye after the Game 4 win over the Spurs and before they hoisted the Larry O’B back in Texas.The MSG faithful will have to wait a couple of weeks for the unveiling of the banner(s?), but it’s not that having the Knickerbockers playing closer to them won’t be welcomed.Here’s the latest from a heated Brown and a few other people before tip-off.On challenging the Knicks’ bench players to compete harder in practice:“I brought it up today, when we weren’t competing. I’m like, you know what? And I specifically went down the line talking about Jalen, Mikal, OG, KAT and Josh. I said those five: they are going to play. If they do something wrong, I’m going to get on them and we’re going to figure it out, but they still are going to play. I said, everybody else in this gym: you [are] fighting.“You’re fighting either to make the team or you’re fighting for minutes. I said, look around. This is not just because we won last year. This has nothing to do with last year’s team. Those five guys are the same. But this is a new year, a new team. We got to look forward. And so, every day, it’s a competition. We should be pushing each other to get better while competing for minutes and/or to make the team. So, you’re 100% accurate. It’s going to be hard.”On how the Warriors avoided complacency after winning the first of two consecutive titles:“There was no slippage. And when I say no slippage, there was no slippage in our process from Year One to Year Two. Guys embraced the details. They embraced the little things. They knew we couldn’t just show up and turn the light switch on and think just because we won last year, we’re going to win this year.“That group was very, very good, and it started with the core players. The core players didn’t allow it to happen, which made it easy for our staff to say what we needed to say when we did start having slippage, because everybody is human, so it’s going to happen.“We have to embrace all the work and the details that go into it along with the effort every single day.”On how winning a championship could affect Mikal Bridges’ confidence and the scrutiny he faces:“It definitely can be freeing. It can definitely help with the validation that every human being looks for in life or in whatever they do. But at the end of the day, everybody has a short-term memory. It’s ‘what can you do for me lately?’ Nobody can ever take that away from any of us because we were all a part of it. But if you want to stay on top, it’s gonna be hard. It’s gonna be even harder. …There’s gonna be more scrutiny. And that scrutiny might even be at a higher level.”On Mike Brown holding the Knicks accountable after a lackluster practice:“I think that’s what makes Coach a great coach, just holding us accountable. It can be human nature to relax a little bit. As a player, as a coach, as a fan, you can relax after having a lot of success. It’s difficult to do something great and continue to try and get better.“And that’s our goal. We did something great last year; it was last year, and I think the biggest thing coming into this year is that we know what it takes.“It’s just great that coach did that, holding us accountable because we want to be the best team we can be. And the best team we can be, we can’t be the same exact team that we were last year. It’s a different team; we gotta be even better. Those lapses where we might get a little human nature in us, where we play a game and have a little day in between and we’re kind of, maybe sometimes going through the motions, it was great for coach to do that to us because the thing about us, we’re all competitors and we all want to win. So as soon as Coach says something like that, none of us are going to back down and be like ‘whatever.’ We’re going to pick it up and keep fighting and get better.”On dealing with criticism and scrutiny following his trade to the Knicks:“I got a phone. Even if I don’t want to see it or anything, it’s always there. That’s just life. People talk about anything, and that’s all right; you just gotta go about your business. People can think however they want to think; I just know that I’m gonna work hard and try to be the best teammate that I can be and best player that I can be and continue to try and help win as much as I can.”On whether he feels fully appreciated by Knicks fans after winning a championship:“I don’t know. I’m not sure about that. Can just say that I’m appreciative of fans. If I see them when I’m walking my dog or something like that, just a lot of nice things to say. That’s foremost, kind of more like a human-to-human interaction, just very nice and grateful to be in this position. I don’t need to feel like there’s validation and there’s like, ‘OK, now he can…’ No, I hold myself accountable at all times.”On how Knicks fans’ expectations have pushed him to improve:“That’s the thing that I do love about this organization and the fans, even though some might be a little more crazy than others, they want the best out of you. I never take that for granted. I talk to myself a lot when I go through a lot of things and I got people that help me as well, but that’s one thing that I do take from it, is that they get the best out of me. When I’m struggling and I know I gotta be better, I can’t hide from it sometimes — even though I know internally, the people let me know as well. As much as you get frustrated about it, the only thing it does is drive me and I continue to try and get better. I’m always appreciative of it.”On the Knicks still having something to prove after winning the championship:“I think we all still have something to prove.”On avoiding complacency and raising the Knicks’ intensity during training camp:“I think throughout the year, we’re gonna have our ups and downs. The first week, second week of training camp, we’ll have days like that, but we just don’t want to get complacent at all. If we continue to try to win every single day, we try to compete every single day — for us [during] training camp, we just wanna pick up the level and be ready for the home opener in two weeks and get it rolling for the regular season.“We just wanted to pick the energy up, keep continuing to play at a high level and pick the physicality up. I think that was a big thing that he said from last game.”On his disappointment with how his LeBron James and Joel Embiid story was interpreted:“I’m so disappointed how the story was interpreted. The whole intent was praising LeBron for already having an impact on the team’s professionalism and accountability, even something so benign as a player getting on the court for practice a minute or two late.”On apologizing for the report and accepting James’ denial:“I thought it would be an interesting anecdote to show LeBron’s leadership already on display in Philly. For me, the fact that the teammate was Joel was meaningless. In hindsight, I should have realized the fact that it was Joel is what made it a story. I’ve always been a huge fan of Joel and feel awful that it put the focus on him the way that it did.“I don’t know why the person who told me the story would make it up, but if LeBron says it never happened then I believe him and apologize for putting it out there.”On choosing between Jalen Brunson and Allen Iverson:“That is a great question that I’m struggling with because I was a big A.I. fan. Jalen Brunson against the odds… my eyes were ready to not embrace him throughout the playoff run, but he just kept saying, ‘Watch this; watch this.’“I might be being a prisoner of this moment because A.I. is Godly to me, God-like, but what Jalen Brunson did to the favoured Spurs… I can’t argue with it.”

item.title: Gran Piemonte: Dorian Godon sprints to victory despite teammate's crash on sketchy final corner
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Dorian Godon (Netcompany Ineos) stormed to victory from the crash-marred sprint which decided the 110th edition of Gran Piemonte, coming back from being dropped on the final climb in the last 10km to fight for his seventh win in 2026 on Thursday. Anthon Charmig (Uno-X Mobility) had hit the front in the sprint, but was overtaken by the Frenchman before the line, with Italy's Alberto Bettiol (XDS Astana) taking third.Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) looked as through he was going to power to back-to-back solo victories at the Italian semi-Classic on Thursday, after his UAE team brought back the day's early breakaway and paced hard for the majority of the 185km race, launching him into a first attack 18km from the finish.The Mexican star dropped everyone on the key La Morra climb in the Langhe hills south of Turin, except for Finn Fisher-Black (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). Fighting through gritted teeth over the top, Del Toro did briefly leave his companion behind with 13km to go, with the large chasing peloton just 28 seconds in arrears. But on the descent towards Bra, Fisher-Black toiled away to get back on the Mexican's wheel in the final 10km.They worked together to try and stay ahead, but as Godon's Ineos team and several others contributed to the chase, the two escapees were brought back with 1.5km to go. As the wind up for a mass sprint started, the twisty roads heading into Bra saw an initial crash with 600 metres to go, and then a second crash around the final, dangerous corner. Godon's teammate Axel Laurance was the first to hit the deck in the crash that took down several riders, but the Frenchman managed to avoid the incident and deliver the win."I didn't have my best feeling, but the team did an amazing job to put me in a good position. Until the last 2km, I just followed Axel and he went super smooth, and I just gave everything after the final turn," said Godon after the finish."I was in third position, I went directly and I still had to recover, it was a super hard finish. I'm so happy, one more race in Paris-Tours and then holiday.Godon has been one of the signings of the season and a huge gem for Ineos, impressing as a versatile puncheur and sprint option."I'm still young, 30 years old for me, and I'm on my best years. The team give 100% for me, so I have a lot more chances than other years, and when I have my chance, I think I'm good," he said, adding this title to previous Italian successes at the Giro del Veneto, Coppa Bernocchi, and Gran Premio del Lazio."I like it [in Italy], twisty finals, a bit chaotic, and like two minutes all out – I'm better to sprint with an effort before, [because] I'm more of a puncher than a sprinter. In Italy, all the towns are up the top of one hill, so all the finish lines are hard, and I like to race here at the end of the season. I'm happy to have another win here, a famous one."Gran Piemonte not only signalled the final race before retirement for two Italian stalwarts of the peloton, Damiano Caruso (Bahrain Victorious) and Jacopo Mosca (Lidl-Trek), but it also wrapped up the build up to the final Monument of the season at Il Lombardia, the showpiece event of the Italian Autumn Classics this Saturday.Dorian Godon (Fra) Ineos GrenadiersAnthon Charmig (Den) Uno-X MobilityAlberto Bettiol (Ita) XDS Astana Lukas Nerurkar (GBr) EF Education-EasyPostQuinten Hermans (Bel) Pinarello-Q36.5Fred Wright (GBr) Pinarello-Q36.5Afonso Eulálio (Por) Bahrain VictoriousMichael Matthews (Aus) Jayco-AlUlaJhonatan Narváez (Ecu) UAE Team Emirates-XRGPau Marti Soriano (Spa) NSN Cycling TeamSimone Gualdi (Ita) Lotto-IntermarchéLaurence Pithie (NZl) Red Bull-Bora-HansgroheJon Barrenetxea Golzarri (Spa) Movistar TeamMatteo Sobrero (Ita) Lidl-TrekFilippo Turconi (Ita) Bardiani-CSF 7 SaberRomain Gregoire (Fra) Groupama-FDJ UnitedPau Miquel Delgado (Spa) Bahrain VictoriousMartin Marcellusi (Ita) Bardiani-CSF 7 SaberWarren Barguil (Fra) Picnic PostNLFabio Christen (Swi) Pinarello-Q36.5Dario Igor Belletta (Ita) Polti-VisitMaltaSam Maisonobe (Fra) CofidisGorka Corres Ibañez De Opakua (Spa) Caja Rural-Seguros RGAMatteo Trentin (Ita) Tudor Pro CyclingFilippo Magli (Ita) Bardiani-CSF 7 SaberFernando Barcelo Aragon (Spa) Caja Rural-Seguros RGARudy Molard (Fra) Groupama-FDJ UnitedJoan Bou Company (Spa) Caja Rural-Seguros RGAFrancesco Busatto (Ita) Alpecin-Premier TechDario Giuliano (Fra) Polti-VisitMaltaSubscribe to Cyclingnews for comprehensive race coverage of the UCI Gravel World Championships, alongside the final Monument of the season, Il Lombardia. item.title: McLaren targets Norris’ costly fuel system issue with Singapore F1 power unit fixes
Hunt joins the ultra-wide crowd with new 5AM Gravel Limitless race wheels
item.author: Emily Tillett
item.content:encoded: Nothing evidences modern gravel racing as clearly as the cohort of aero gravel wheels that have launched in the past few years. We've seen ultra-wide aero gravel wheels from the likes of Zipp and Enve, and now British brand Hunt has joined the party with its new 5AM Gravel Limitless wheels, or 5AMG for short. That extra width isn't just about accommodating bigger tyres. By creating a wider rim profile, the transition between a high-volume tyre and the carbon rim is smoother, helping to reduce aerodynamic drag.The wheels have been used in racing for a couple of months now, and we've already had them in the wind tunnel as part of our recent CN Labs showdown where we put some of the latest deep-section gravel wheels to the test.It's well known that wider tyres are well suited to rough terrain, offering greater comfort and control, but their increased size also makes them naturally less aerodynamic. That leaves wheel designers needing to create rims wide enough to accommodate increasingly large gravel tyres while still minimising aerodynamic drag, and without adding too much weight in the process.So, how has Hunt gone about solving that problem?According to Hunt, the 5AMG Limitless was designed to balance several competing demands from aerodynamic efficiency and low weight to tyre protection and stability in changing wind conditions.The result is a wheelset with a deeper, wider front wheel where clean airflow matters more, and a shallower, narrower rear wheel where Hunt has prioritised weight and responsiveness.The front rim is 54mm deep and 45mm wide, while the rear is 49mm deep and 38mm wide. Both have a 27mm internal rim width and the brand has optimised the wheels for 45mm and 50mm tyre setups, though they are compatible with 40-60mm hookless tyres. The more aero a wheelset is, the heavier it tends to be, so keeping the weight down was another priority for Hunt.There are two build options built around the 'Aero Maximised' rim with the option of carbon or stainless steel spokes. The carbon-spoke version has a claimed weight of 1,317g per pair, while the stainless steel version comes in at 1,447g. The stainless steel version uses Pillar Super Wing bladed spokes with internal nipples, which Hunt says have been designed to minimise turbulence and make this its most aerodynamic stainless steel spoke and hidden-nipple combination to date.The 5AMG Limitless Ti_UD carbon spoke version was the lightest wheelset in Hunt's own wind tunnel testing and also recorded the lowest drag.Hunt has also used its Limitless technology which incorporates a low-density polymer filler in the rim's bead which it says allows them to create a wider rim profile without adding significant weight.Pinch flat protection was another consideration, with the 5AMG using extra-wide rim beads measuring 9mm at the front and 5.5mm at the rear. This is significantly wider than most wheels on the market, even gravel wheels. Hunt says the wider beads help 'fend off race-ending pinch flats' while also adding structural strength to the rim profile to protect against rock strikes. You can pre-order the new 5AMG wheelsets now, with delivery slated for December 1st. Hunt offers a lifetime crash repair or replacement policy, too.The pricing is as follows:5AMG Limitless Steel Spoke Wheelset 5AMG Limitless Ti_UD Carbon Spoke Wheelset 5AMG Limitless Ti_UD Carbon Spoke Wheelset (CeramicSpeed Alpha)

item.title: Isaac del Toro reveals mystery knee pain ahead of trying to defend Pogačar's Il Lombardia streak alongside World Champion Brandon McNulty for UAE
item.author: James Moultrie
item.content:encoded: Despite going without their talisman Tadej Pogačar for the final Monument of the season at Il Lombardia, UAE Team Emirates-XRG will still be starting with one of the strongest lineups, led by new World Champion Brandon McNulty and Mexican star Isaac del Toro.The latter was fifth on debut last season, while the US rider hasn't raced the Autumn Classic since 2021, when he supported the Slovenian en route to his first of five consecutive wins, matching Fausto Coppi's 72-year-old record just 12 months ago. With a stacked start list to contend with if they are to maintain the team's run of victories, UAE are also bringing former podium finisher Adam Yates to the start, alongside Jan Christen, Felix Großschartner, Domen Novak, and Pavel Sivakov.Their main rivals will include Remco Evenepoel, Primož Roglič (both Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5), Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM), Giulio Ciccone (Lidl-Trek), Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost), and Matteo Jorgenson (Visma-Lease a Bike)."We go into Lombardia as defending champions and we’ll have a clear goal to keep that title. The team is very strong and we have many options for victory," said Del Toro on the UAE team's website."Obviously Brandon is flying in the rainbows at the moment and personally I’m in good form also. The key will be to have numbers as deep into the race as possible and then play our cards on the road."We have a good feeling in the group and understand each other well, so it puts us in a strong position from the start. The rest will depend on the rivals."Since Worlds, McNulty has brought his rainbow jersey to life with impressive, attacking performances at the Giro dell'Emilia, Coppa Agostoni, and Tre Valli Varesine, finishing 10th, second, and 23rd. And while he had been feeling the effects of his stunning solo win in Montreal, Del Toro's presence makes the opportunistic attack late in the finale just as possible as it was in Canada – but nothing can represent more of a target on one's back than the rainbow jersey itself.But unfortunately for team boss Mauro Gianetti's men, they have one small issue in the form of an unknown knee problem for Del Toro, which he revealed at the start of Gran Piemonte on Thursday morning. It should become clear after the 185km 1.Pro race whether or not he has been significantly affected, hoping to carry the form which saw him attack Worlds as one of the main aggressors, eventually finishing fifth behind his trade teammate. "[I'm] good, battling with the jet lag and also the knee pain, but hopefully now we will be OK. So let's see how the legs are, and of course we try to do our best today," Del Toro told CyclingProNet at the start in Asti.Asked to clarify the knee issues, he said: "[It hurts] a little bit, I don't know why. After the travel, I started to have some troubles – I had the same bike, same shoes, same everything, but I don't know – just let's see how I am and, of course, in the race, hopefully I feel good and can do my job."I need to play alongside Johnny [Narváez] and Brandon [McNulty]; they both are flying on these types of parcours. Of course we need to play the cards well, and I need to be alongside them, but we'll see how the race develops and well try to do it."22-year-old Del Toro extended his contract with UAE earlier this year until the end of 2031, signalling him as the Emirati squad's long-term leader after Pogačar, and after two incredible opening years on cycling's best team, he has only kicked on to bigger and better things in 2026. He's managed GC victories at the UAE Tour, Tirreno-Adriatico, and the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, took third on GC on debut at the Tour de France – while supporting the Slovenian to overall victory, and has won the GP de Montreal. Del Toro is expected to fill Pogačar's shoes when he eventually winds down his career, and he will have an early chance to taste some of that ultimate responsibility this weekend, as long as this knee pain doesn't turn into a bigger issue.
